article_steps.title: What is a Merge Conflict?
article_steps.content: A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine changes from two branches. This usually occurs when the same line in a file has been modified differently in each branch.

article_steps.title: Why Do Conflicts Happen?
article_steps.content: Conflicts arise when two branches modify the same part of a file. Git doesn't know which change to keep, so it marks the conflict and asks you to resolve it manually.

article_steps.title: Step 1: Start the Merge
article_steps.content: When you attempt to merge a branch and there is a conflict, Git will stop and show you a message like 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in filename'.
article_steps.command: git merge feature-branch

article_steps.title: Step 2: Find Conflicting Files
article_steps.content: Use git status to see which files have conflicts. They will be listed under 'Unmerged paths'.
article_steps.command: git status

article_steps.title: Step 3: Open and Edit the Conflicting File
article_steps.content:
Open the file in your text editor. You will see conflict markers like this:

<<<<<<< HEAD
Your changes
=======
Their changes
>>>>>>> feature-branch

Decide which changes to keep, remove the conflict markers, and save the file.

article_steps.title: Step 4: Mark as Resolved and Commit
article_steps.content: After resolving all conflicts, add the files and commit:
article_steps.command:
git add .
git commit -m "Resolved merge conflicts"

article_steps.title: How to Verify
article_steps.content: Run git log to confirm the merge commit was created successfully:
article_steps.command: git log --oneline -5

article_steps.title: Understanding the Error
article_steps.content: The error 'failed to push some refs to remote' means that the remote branch has commits that your local branch doesn't have. Git prevents you from pushing to avoid losing those commits.

article_steps.title: Step 1: Pull the Latest Changes
article_steps.content: First, pull the latest changes from the remote branch and merge them into your local branch:
article_steps.command: git pull origin main

article_steps.title: Step 2: Resolve Any Conflicts
article_steps.content: If there are merge conflicts after pulling, resolve them as described in our merge conflicts guide, then commit the resolved files.

article_steps.title: Step 3: Push Again
article_steps.content: After pulling and resolving any conflicts, push your changes again:
article_steps.command: git push origin main

article_steps.title: Alternative: Force Push (Use with Caution)
article_steps.content: If you are sure you want to overwrite the remote branch, you can force push. WARNING: This will overwrite the remote branch and may cause other developers to lose their work.
article_steps.command: git push --force origin main

article_steps.title: Why Authentication Fails
article_steps.content: Since August 2021, GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations. You must use either a Personal Access Token (PAT) or SSH key authentication.

article_steps.title: Option 1: Personal Access Token (PAT)
article_steps.content: Go to GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Generate new token. Select the required scopes (at minimum, 'repo') and generate the token. Copy it immediately — you won't see it again.

article_steps.title: Use the Token
article_steps.content: When Git asks for your password, paste the Personal Access Token instead. You can also update your remote URL to include the token:
article_steps.command: git remote set-url origin https://YOUR_TOKEN@github.com/username/repo.git

article_steps.title: Option 2: SSH Key Authentication
article_steps.content: Generate a new SSH key pair on your computer:
article_steps.command: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com"

article_steps.title: Add SSH Key to GitHub
article_steps.content: Copy your public key and add it to GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key:
article_steps.command:
# Copy the public key:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Then switch your remote URL to SSH:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/repo.git

article_steps.title: Verify SSH Connection
article_steps.content: Test your SSH connection to GitHub:
article_steps.command: ssh -T git@github.com

article_steps.title: What are Branches?
article_steps.content: Branches allow you to work on different features or fixes independently. The default branch is usually called 'main' or 'master'. You create new branches to isolate your work.

article_steps.title: Create a New Branch
article_steps.content: Use the git branch command followed by the name of your new branch:
article_steps.command: git branch feature-login

article_steps.title: Switch to the New Branch
article_steps.content: Switch to your newly created branch using git switch (modern) or git checkout (traditional):
article_steps.command:
# Modern way:
git switch feature-login

# Traditional way:
git checkout feature-login

article_steps.title: Create and Switch in One Command
article_steps.content: You can create a new branch and switch to it in a single command:
article_steps.command:
# Modern way:
git switch -c feature-login

# Traditional way:
git checkout -b feature-login

article_steps.title: List All Branches
article_steps.content: To see all branches in your repository, use:
article_steps.command:
git branch
# The current branch is marked with an asterisk (*)

article_steps.title: Key Difference
article_steps.content: git reset removes commits from history (rewrites history). git revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit (preserves history). Use reset for local changes and revert for shared branches.

article_steps.title: Git Reset (Rewrites History)
article_steps.content: Reset moves the branch pointer backward, effectively removing commits. There are three modes:
article_steps.command:
# Keep changes in working directory and staging:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Keep changes in working directory only:
git reset --mixed HEAD~1

# Discard all changes completely:
git reset --hard HEAD~1

article_steps.title: Git Revert (Preserves History)
article_steps.content: Revert creates a new commit that undoes the changes from a specific commit. This is safe to use on shared branches because it doesn't rewrite history.
article_steps.command:
git revert HEAD
# or revert a specific commit:
git revert abc1234

article_steps.title: When to Use Which
article_steps.content:
Use git reset when:
- Working locally and haven't pushed yet
- Want to clean up messy local commits

Use git revert when:
- Changes have been pushed to a shared branch
- You need to preserve the commit history
- Working in a team

article_steps.title: Undo Commit, Keep Changes Staged
article_steps.content: This is the safest option. It removes the commit but keeps your changes ready to be committed again:
article_steps.command: git reset --soft HEAD~1

article_steps.title: Undo Commit, Unstage Changes
article_steps.content: This removes the commit and unstages the files, but keeps your changes in the working directory:
article_steps.command:
git reset HEAD~1
# or explicitly:
git reset --mixed HEAD~1

article_steps.title: Undo Commit and Discard All Changes
article_steps.content: WARNING: This permanently deletes your changes. Use only if you're sure:
article_steps.command: git reset --hard HEAD~1

article_steps.title: Just Fix the Commit Message
article_steps.content: If you only need to change the commit message, use amend:
article_steps.command: git commit --amend -m "New corrected commit message"

article_steps.title: What is Cloning?
article_steps.content: Cloning creates a local copy of a remote repository on your computer. It downloads all files, branches, and commit history.

article_steps.title: Clone Using HTTPS
article_steps.content: Go to the repository on GitHub, click the green 'Code' button, copy the HTTPS URL, and run:
article_steps.command: git clone https://github.com/username/repository.git

article_steps.title: Clone Using SSH
article_steps.content: If you have SSH set up (see our authentication guide), use the SSH URL:
article_steps.command: git clone git@github.com:username/repository.git

article_steps.title: Clone to a Specific Folder
article_steps.content: You can specify a folder name after the URL:
article_steps.command: git clone https://github.com/username/repository.git my-folder

article_steps.title: What is the Staging Area?
article_steps.content: The staging area (also called the index) is a space between your working directory and the repository. You use 'git add' to move changes to the staging area before committing them.

article_steps.title: Stage a Single File
article_steps.content: Add a specific file to the staging area:
article_steps.command: git add filename.txt

article_steps.title: Stage All Changes
article_steps.content: Add all modified and new files to staging:
article_steps.command:
git add .
# or:
git add --all

article_steps.title: Check What is Staged
article_steps.content: Use git status to see which files are staged and which are not:
article_steps.command: git status

article_steps.title: Unstage a File
article_steps.content: If you accidentally staged a file, you can unstage it:
article_steps.command: git restore --staged filename.txt

article_steps.title: Why Commit Messages Matter
article_steps.content: Good commit messages help you and your team understand what changed and why. They make debugging easier and create a useful project history.

article_steps.title: Basic Commit with Message
article_steps.content: Use the -m flag to add a message to your commit:
article_steps.command: git commit -m "Add user login form validation"

article_steps.title: Follow the Convention
article_steps.content:
A good commit message format:

1. Start with a verb (Add, Fix, Update, Remove, Refactor)
2. Keep the subject line under 50 characters
3. Use the imperative mood ('Add feature' not 'Added feature')
4. Capitalize the first letter
5. Don't end with a period

article_steps.title: Examples of Good vs Bad Messages
article_steps.content:
Good:
- Add user authentication with JWT
- Fix null pointer error in checkout flow
- Update README with installation steps

Bad:
- fixed stuff
- update
- asdfasdf
- WIP

article_steps.title: View Commit History
article_steps.content: Use git log to see your commit messages:
article_steps.command: git log --oneline -10

article_steps.title: What is the Reflog?
article_steps.content: The reflog (reference log) records every change to your branch tips and HEAD. Even if you delete a commit with 'git reset --hard', the commit still exists in the reflog for about 90 days.

article_steps.title: View the Reflog
article_steps.content: See the history of all HEAD movements:
article_steps.command: git reflog

article_steps.title: Find the Lost Commit
article_steps.content:
The reflog shows entries like:
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add login feature

The hash 'def5678' is the commit you lost.

article_steps.title: Recover the Commit
article_steps.content: Use git reset to move your branch back to the lost commit:
article_steps.command:
# Reset to the lost commit:
git reset --hard def5678

# Or cherry-pick it onto your current branch:
git cherry-pick def5678

article_steps.title: What is Git Stash?
article_steps.content: Git stash takes your uncommitted changes (both staged and unstaged) and saves them on a stack. Your working directory becomes clean, allowing you to switch branches or pull updates.

article_steps.title: Stash Your Changes
article_steps.content: Save your current changes to the stash:
article_steps.command:
git stash
# or with a descriptive message:
git stash save "Work in progress on login form"

article_steps.title: Restore Stashed Changes
article_steps.content: Apply the most recent stash and remove it from the stack:
article_steps.command: git stash pop

article_steps.title: List All Stashes
article_steps.content: View all items in your stash stack:
article_steps.command: git stash list

article_steps.title: Apply a Specific Stash
article_steps.content: Apply a specific stash without removing it from the list:
article_steps.command: git stash apply stash@{2}

article_steps.title: What is a Remote?
article_steps.content: A remote is a connection to another copy of your repository, usually hosted on a platform like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The default remote is typically called 'origin'.

article_steps.title: View Remotes
article_steps.content: See all configured remotes and their URLs:
article_steps.command: git remote -v

article_steps.title: Add a New Remote
article_steps.content: Connect your local repo to a remote repository:
article_steps.command: git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git

article_steps.title: Change Remote URL
article_steps.content: Update the URL of an existing remote:
article_steps.command: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/username/new-repo.git

article_steps.title: Remove a Remote
article_steps.content: Disconnect a remote from your local repo:
article_steps.command: git remote remove origin

article_steps.title: Why Use SSH Keys?
article_steps.content: SSH keys provide secure authentication without typing passwords. Once set up, Git operations with GitHub are seamless and secure.

article_steps.title: Generate an SSH Key
article_steps.content: Create a new SSH key pair using the Ed25519 algorithm (recommended):
article_steps.command: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com"

article_steps.title: Start the SSH Agent
article_steps.content: Start the SSH agent and add your key:
article_steps.command:
# Start the agent:
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

# Add your key:
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

article_steps.title: Copy the Public Key
article_steps.content: Copy your public key to the clipboard:
article_steps.command:
# Mac:
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Windows:
clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Linux:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

article_steps.title: Add Key to GitHub
article_steps.content: Go to GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key. Paste your public key and give it a descriptive title.

article_steps.title: Test the Connection
article_steps.content: Verify that SSH authentication is working:
article_steps.command:
ssh -T git@github.com
# Expected: Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...

article_steps.title: Git Fetch vs Git Pull
article_steps.content: git fetch downloads changes from the remote but does NOT merge them into your working branch. git pull does both — it fetches AND merges in one step. Think of pull as fetch + merge.

article_steps.title: Using Git Fetch
article_steps.content: Download remote changes without modifying your working directory:
article_steps.command:
git fetch origin
# Then review what changed:
git log origin/main --oneline -5

article_steps.title: Using Git Pull
article_steps.content: Download and immediately merge remote changes:
article_steps.command: git pull origin main

article_steps.title: Pull with Rebase
article_steps.content: Instead of creating a merge commit, you can rebase your local commits on top of the fetched changes for a cleaner history:
article_steps.command: git pull --rebase origin main

article_steps.title: What is Git Push?
article_steps.content: Git push uploads your local commits to a remote repository. This shares your work with others and backs up your code.

article_steps.title: Push to Remote
article_steps.content: Push your current branch to the remote repository:
article_steps.command: git push origin main

article_steps.title: Set Upstream and Push
article_steps.content: The first time you push a new branch, set the upstream tracking:
article_steps.command:
git push -u origin feature-branch
# After this, you can just use:
git push

article_steps.title: Push All Branches
article_steps.content: Push all local branches to the remote:
article_steps.command: git push --all origin

article_steps.title: What is Detached HEAD?
article_steps.content: Normally, HEAD points to a branch name (like 'main'). In detached HEAD state, HEAD points directly to a specific commit instead of a branch. This usually happens when you checkout a specific commit hash.

article_steps.title: How Did This Happen?
article_steps.content: You likely ran something like:
article_steps.command:
git checkout abc1234
# This detaches HEAD from any branch

article_steps.title: Go Back to a Branch
article_steps.content: The simplest fix is to switch back to an existing branch:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
# or:
git checkout main

article_steps.title: Save Your Work as a New Branch
article_steps.content: If you made commits in detached HEAD state and want to keep them, create a new branch:
article_steps.command:
git switch -c my-saved-work
# or:
git checkout -b my-saved-work

article_steps.title: Delete a Local Branch
article_steps.content: After merging a branch, delete it locally to keep your repository clean:
article_steps.command:
# Safe delete (only if merged):
git branch -d feature-branch

# Force delete (even if not merged):
git branch -D feature-branch

article_steps.title: Delete a Remote Branch
article_steps.content: Remove a branch from the remote repository:
article_steps.command: git push origin --delete feature-branch

article_steps.title: Clean Up Remote Tracking Branches
article_steps.content: Remove references to remote branches that no longer exist:
article_steps.command: git fetch --prune

article_steps.title: What is Merging?
article_steps.content: Merging combines the changes from one branch into another. It's how you bring your feature work back into the main branch.

article_steps.title: Basic Merge
article_steps.content: First switch to the branch you want to merge INTO (usually main), then merge:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git merge feature-branch

article_steps.title: Fast-Forward vs Three-Way Merge
article_steps.content: If the main branch hasn't changed since the feature branch was created, Git does a fast-forward merge (moves the pointer forward). If both branches have new commits, Git creates a merge commit (three-way merge).

article_steps.title: Force a Merge Commit
article_steps.content: If you want a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible (useful for keeping history clear):
article_steps.command: git merge --no-ff feature-branch

article_steps.title: Squash Merge
article_steps.content: Combine all commits from a branch into a single commit:
article_steps.command:
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "Add feature: user login"

article_steps.title: What is Forking?
article_steps.content: Forking creates a personal copy of someone else's repository on your GitHub account. You can freely experiment in your fork without affecting the original project.

article_steps.title: Step 1: Fork the Repository
article_steps.content: Go to the repository on GitHub and click the 'Fork' button in the top-right corner. GitHub creates a copy in your account.

article_steps.title: Step 2: Clone Your Fork
article_steps.content: Clone your forked repository to your local machine:
article_steps.command:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/repository.git
cd repository

article_steps.title: Step 3: Add Upstream Remote
article_steps.content: Add the original repository as a remote called 'upstream' to stay synced:
article_steps.command: git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/repository.git

article_steps.title: Step 4: Create a Feature Branch
article_steps.content: Create a new branch for your contribution:
article_steps.command: git switch -c fix-typo-in-readme

article_steps.title: Step 5: Push and Create Pull Request
article_steps.content: After making changes and committing, push to your fork and create a pull request on GitHub:
article_steps.command:
git push origin fix-typo-in-readme
# Then go to GitHub and click 'Create Pull Request'

article_steps.title: Create on GitHub
article_steps.content: Go to GitHub, click the '+' button in the top-right corner, and select 'New repository'. Give it a name, choose public or private, and click 'Create repository'.

article_steps.title: Connect Local Project
article_steps.content: If you already have a local project, connect it to the new GitHub repository:
article_steps.command:
cd my-project
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git
git push -u origin main

article_steps.title: Or Clone the Empty Repo
article_steps.content: If you're starting fresh, clone the empty repository:
article_steps.command:
git clone https://github.com/username/repo.git
cd repo

article_steps.title: What is .gitignore?
article_steps.content: A .gitignore file tells Git which files or directories to ignore. This is useful for keeping build files, dependencies, and sensitive information out of your repository.

article_steps.title: Create a .gitignore File
article_steps.content: Create a file named .gitignore in the root of your repository. Add patterns for files to ignore:
article_steps.command:
# Example .gitignore contents:
node_modules/
.env
*.log
dist/
.DS_Store

article_steps.title: Stop Tracking an Already Tracked File
article_steps.content: If a file is already being tracked, add it to .gitignore and then remove it from tracking:
article_steps.command:
git rm --cached filename.txt
git commit -m "Stop tracking filename.txt"

article_steps.title: What is Cherry-Pick?
article_steps.content: Cherry-pick allows you to apply the changes from a specific commit to your current branch. Unlike merge, it picks individual commits rather than merging an entire branch.

article_steps.title: Find the Commit Hash
article_steps.content: First, find the hash of the commit you want to pick:
article_steps.command: git log --oneline feature-branch

article_steps.title: Cherry-Pick the Commit
article_steps.content: Apply the commit to your current branch:
article_steps.command: git cherry-pick abc1234

article_steps.title: Cherry-Pick Without Committing
article_steps.content: Apply the changes without creating a commit (useful if you want to modify first):
article_steps.command: git cherry-pick --no-commit abc1234

article_steps.title: Basic Log
article_steps.content: View the full commit history with details:
article_steps.command: git log

article_steps.title: Compact One-Line Log
article_steps.content: See a condensed history with short commit hashes:
article_steps.command: git log --oneline

article_steps.title: Visual Branch Graph
article_steps.content: See a visual representation of branch history:
article_steps.command: git log --oneline --graph --all

article_steps.title: Search Commit Messages
article_steps.content: Find commits with specific keywords:
article_steps.command: git log --grep="login"

article_steps.title: What is Git Diff?
article_steps.content: Git diff shows the differences between various states of your repository. It compares file contents line by line and shows exactly what was added, modified, or removed. Lines prefixed with '+' are additions and lines prefixed with '-' are deletions.

article_steps.title: Compare Working Directory to Staging
article_steps.content: See changes you have made but not yet staged:
article_steps.command: git diff

article_steps.title: Compare Staging Area to Last Commit
article_steps.content: See changes that are staged and ready to be committed:
article_steps.command:
git diff --staged
# or the older synonym:
git diff --cached

article_steps.title: Compare Working Directory to Last Commit
article_steps.content: See all changes since the last commit, whether staged or not:
article_steps.command: git diff HEAD

article_steps.title: Compare Two Branches
article_steps.content: See the differences between two branches:
article_steps.command:
git diff main..feature-branch
# Or see just the file names:
git diff --name-only main..feature-branch

article_steps.title: Compare a Specific File
article_steps.content: Limit the diff output to a single file:
article_steps.command: git diff -- path/to/file.txt

article_steps.title: What Does Git Status Show?
article_steps.content: Git status displays the state of your working directory and staging area. It tells you which changes have been staged, which haven't, and which files aren't being tracked by Git.

article_steps.title: Basic Status
article_steps.content: Run git status to see the full status report:
article_steps.command: git status

article_steps.title: Understanding the Output
article_steps.content:
Git status groups files into three categories:

1. Changes to be committed (staged) – shown in green
2. Changes not staged for commit (modified but unstaged) – shown in red
3. Untracked files (new files Git doesn't know about) – shown in red

article_steps.title: Short Status Format
article_steps.content: Get a compact one-line-per-file view:
article_steps.command:
git status -s
# Output codes: M = modified, A = added, D = deleted, ?? = untracked
# Left column = staged, Right column = unstaged

article_steps.title: Show Branch Info
article_steps.content: Include tracking branch information:
article_steps.command:
git status -b
# Shows how many commits ahead/behind your tracking branch

article_steps.title: Config Levels
article_steps.content:
Git has three configuration levels:

1. System (/etc/gitconfig) – applies to all users
2. Global (~/.gitconfig) – applies to your user account
3. Local (.git/config) – applies to the current repository only

Local overrides global, which overrides system.

article_steps.title: Set Your Default Editor
article_steps.content: Change the default text editor Git uses for commit messages:
article_steps.command:
# Use VS Code:
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

# Use Nano:
git config --global core.editor "nano"

# Use Vim:
git config --global core.editor "vim"

article_steps.title: Set Default Branch Name
article_steps.content: Change the default branch name for new repositories from 'master' to 'main':
article_steps.command: git config --global init.defaultBranch main

article_steps.title: Enable Auto-Coloring
article_steps.content: Make Git output colorful and easier to read:
article_steps.command: git config --global color.ui auto

article_steps.title: Configure Line Endings
article_steps.content: Handle line endings correctly across different operating systems:
article_steps.command:
# On Windows:
git config --global core.autocrlf true

# On Mac/Linux:
git config --global core.autocrlf input

article_steps.title: View All Configuration
article_steps.content: List all your current Git configuration settings:
article_steps.command: git config --list --show-origin

article_steps.title: What is HEAD?
article_steps.content: HEAD is a pointer that tells Git which commit you are currently working on. Think of it as 'you are here' on a map. Usually, HEAD points to a branch name (like 'main'), and that branch points to the latest commit.

article_steps.title: See Where HEAD Points
article_steps.content: Check what HEAD currently references:
article_steps.command:
git log --oneline -1
# Or see the raw reference:
cat .git/HEAD

article_steps.title: HEAD vs Branch vs Commit
article_steps.content:
HEAD → points to a branch (e.g., main)
Branch → points to a commit (e.g., abc1234)

When you make a new commit, the branch moves forward and HEAD follows because it points to the branch.

article_steps.title: HEAD Relatives
article_steps.content: You can reference previous commits relative to HEAD:
article_steps.command:
# One commit before HEAD:
git show HEAD~1

# Two commits before HEAD:
git show HEAD~2

# The parent of a merge commit (second parent):
git show HEAD^2

article_steps.title: What is Detached HEAD?
article_steps.content: When HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch, you are in 'detached HEAD' state. This happens when you checkout a specific commit hash. Any commits you make won't belong to any branch unless you create one.

article_steps.title: What are Git Aliases?
article_steps.content: Git aliases are custom shortcuts for frequently used commands. Instead of typing long commands every time, you can create short abbreviations that expand automatically.

article_steps.title: Create Basic Aliases
article_steps.content: Set up common aliases to save time:
article_steps.command:
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.ci commit
git config --global alias.st status

article_steps.title: Use Your Aliases
article_steps.content: Now you can use shorter commands:
article_steps.command:
# Instead of 'git status':
git st

# Instead of 'git checkout main':
git co main

# Instead of 'git branch':
git br

article_steps.title: Create Advanced Aliases
article_steps.content: Create aliases for complex commands you use frequently:
article_steps.command:
# Pretty log graph:
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate"

# Undo last commit (keep changes):
git config --global alias.undo "reset --soft HEAD~1"

# Show last commit:
git config --global alias.last "log -1 HEAD"

article_steps.title: List All Aliases
article_steps.content: View all your configured aliases:
article_steps.command: git config --get-regexp alias

article_steps.title: What are Git Tags?
article_steps.content: Tags are references that point to specific commits, typically used to mark release versions (v1.0.0, v2.1.3). Unlike branches, tags don't move when new commits are made. There are two types: lightweight tags (just a pointer) and annotated tags (full objects with metadata).

article_steps.title: Create a Lightweight Tag
article_steps.content: Create a simple tag pointing to the current commit:
article_steps.command: git tag v1.0.0

article_steps.title: Create an Annotated Tag
article_steps.content: Create a tag with a message, tagger name, and date (recommended for releases):
article_steps.command: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"

article_steps.title: List and View Tags
article_steps.content: See all tags and inspect a specific one:
article_steps.command:
# List all tags:
git tag

# List tags matching a pattern:
git tag -l "v1.*"

# Show tag details:
git show v1.0.0

article_steps.title: Push Tags to Remote
article_steps.content: Tags are not pushed automatically. Push them explicitly:
article_steps.command:
# Push a specific tag:
git push origin v1.0.0

# Push all tags:
git push --tags

article_steps.title: Delete a Tag
article_steps.content: Remove a tag locally and from the remote:
article_steps.command:
# Delete locally:
git tag -d v1.0.0

# Delete from remote:
git push origin --delete v1.0.0

article_steps.title: What is Git Blame?
article_steps.content: Git blame shows the revision and author that last modified each line of a file. It is invaluable for understanding why a line of code exists and who to ask about it. Despite the name, it is not about assigning blame — it is about understanding history.

article_steps.title: Blame a File
article_steps.content: See who last changed each line:
article_steps.command: git blame filename.js

article_steps.title: Blame Specific Lines
article_steps.content: Focus on a range of lines to reduce output:
article_steps.command:
git blame -L 10,20 filename.js
# Shows blame for lines 10 through 20

article_steps.title: Ignore Whitespace Changes
article_steps.content: Skip cosmetic changes like reformatting:
article_steps.command: git blame -w filename.js

article_steps.title: Show the Commit That Changed a Line
article_steps.content: Once you have a commit hash from blame, inspect it:
article_steps.command: git show abc1234

article_steps.title: What is Git Show?
article_steps.content: Git show displays detailed information about a Git object — usually a commit. It shows the commit message, author, date, and the full diff of changes introduced by that commit.

article_steps.title: Show the Latest Commit
article_steps.content: View the most recent commit with its diff:
article_steps.command: git show

article_steps.title: Show a Specific Commit
article_steps.content: Inspect any commit by its hash:
article_steps.command: git show abc1234

article_steps.title: Show Only the Files Changed
article_steps.content: List only the file names without the diff:
article_steps.command: git show --stat abc1234

article_steps.title: Show a File at a Specific Commit
article_steps.content: View the contents of a file as it was at a particular commit:
article_steps.command: git show abc1234:path/to/file.js

article_steps.title: Why Stage Partially?
article_steps.content: Sometimes you make multiple changes to a single file but want to split them into separate commits. Git add -p lets you review each change (called a 'hunk') and choose which ones to stage.

article_steps.title: Start Interactive Staging
article_steps.content: Enter patch mode for a file:
article_steps.command:
git add -p filename.js
# Or for all files:
git add -p

article_steps.title: Understanding the Options
article_steps.content:
For each hunk, Git asks what to do:

y = stage this hunk
n = skip this hunk
q = quit (don't stage remaining hunks)
a = stage this and all remaining hunks
d = skip this and all remaining hunks
s = split this hunk into smaller pieces
e = manually edit this hunk

article_steps.title: Verify What Was Staged
article_steps.content: After selecting hunks, verify your staging area:
article_steps.command:
git diff --staged
# This shows only the parts you staged

article_steps.title: Commit the Staged Changes
article_steps.content: Commit just the selected changes:
article_steps.command:
git commit -m "Fix validation logic"
# The remaining unstaged changes stay in your working directory

article_steps.title: Why Workflows Matter
article_steps.content: A Git workflow defines how your team uses branches, merges, and releases. Choosing the right workflow reduces conflicts, speeds up development, and keeps your repository organized.

article_steps.title: Centralized Workflow
article_steps.content: Everyone works on a single branch (usually main). Simple but risky for teams because one broken commit affects everyone. Best for solo developers or very small teams.

article_steps.title: Feature Branch Workflow
article_steps.content: Each new feature gets its own branch. Developers work in isolation and merge back into main when ready. This is the most common workflow for small-to-medium teams.
article_steps.command:
git switch -c feature/user-auth
# Work, commit, then merge:
git switch main
git merge feature/user-auth

article_steps.title: Gitflow Workflow
article_steps.content:
A structured workflow with specific branch types:
- main: production-ready code
- develop: integration branch
- feature/*: new features
- release/*: release preparation
- hotfix/*: urgent production fixes

Best for projects with scheduled releases.

article_steps.title: Trunk-Based Development
article_steps.content: Developers commit directly to main (or merge very short-lived branches). Relies on feature flags and continuous integration. Used by companies like Google and Facebook for rapid deployment.

article_steps.title: Choosing a Workflow
article_steps.content:
Small team, simple project → Feature Branch
Larger team, scheduled releases → Gitflow
Continuous deployment, experienced team → Trunk-Based
Solo developer → Centralized or Feature Branch

article_steps.title: Git Init – Create from Scratch
article_steps.content: Use git init when you are starting a brand new project that does not exist on any remote server yet:
article_steps.command:
mkdir my-new-project
cd my-new-project
git init

article_steps.title: Git Clone – Copy Existing
article_steps.content: Use git clone when a repository already exists on GitHub or another server and you want a local copy:
article_steps.command: git clone https://github.com/username/existing-repo.git

article_steps.title: Key Differences
article_steps.content:
git init:
- Creates an empty repository
- No remote configured
- No existing history
- You must add a remote manually

git clone:
- Copies entire repository with full history
- Remote 'origin' automatically configured
- All branches available
- Ready to push/pull immediately

article_steps.title: After Git Init – Connect to Remote
article_steps.content: If you used init and want to push to GitHub, add a remote:
article_steps.command:
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git
git push -u origin main

article_steps.title: What are Git Hooks?
article_steps.content: Git hooks are scripts that run automatically before or after Git events like commit, push, and merge. They live in the .git/hooks directory and can be used to enforce coding standards, run tests, or send notifications.

article_steps.title: Available Hooks
article_steps.content:
Common hooks include:

pre-commit: Runs before a commit is created (lint code, run tests)
commit-msg: Validate or modify commit messages
pre-push: Runs before pushing (run test suite)
post-merge: Runs after a successful merge (install dependencies)
pre-rebase: Runs before a rebase starts

article_steps.title: Create a Pre-Commit Hook
article_steps.content: Create a hook that runs linting before every commit:
article_steps.command:
# Create the hook file:
cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit << 'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "Running linter..."
npm run lint
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Linting failed. Commit aborted."
  exit 1
fi
EOF

# Make it executable:
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

article_steps.title: Important Notes
article_steps.content: Hooks in .git/hooks are NOT version-controlled (the .git directory is not pushed). To share hooks with your team, use tools like Husky (for Node.js projects) or store them in a separate directory and symlink them.

article_steps.title: Using Husky for Team Hooks
article_steps.content: Husky makes it easy to share Git hooks through your package.json:
article_steps.command:
npx husky-init && npm install
# This creates a .husky directory with a pre-commit hook

article_steps.title: What is Rebase?
article_steps.content: Rebase takes the commits from your current branch and replays them on top of another branch. Unlike merge, which creates a merge commit, rebase creates a linear history as if you wrote your changes after the latest commit on the target branch.

article_steps.title: Basic Rebase
article_steps.content: Move your feature branch commits on top of the latest main:
article_steps.command:
git switch feature-branch
git rebase main

article_steps.title: Handle Rebase Conflicts
article_steps.content: If conflicts arise during rebase, Git pauses and asks you to resolve them:
article_steps.command:
# Fix the conflicting files, then:
git add .
git rebase --continue

# Or abort the rebase entirely:
git rebase --abort

article_steps.title: The Golden Rule of Rebase
article_steps.content: WARNING: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch. Rebase rewrites commit history, which creates problems for anyone who has already based work on those commits. Only rebase your own local, unpushed commits.

article_steps.title: Rebase vs Merge
article_steps.content:
Use rebase for:
- Cleaning up local commits before merging
- Keeping a linear project history
- Feature branches before creating a pull request

Use merge for:
- Shared branches (main, develop)
- Preserving the exact history of how features were integrated

article_steps.title: Rebase onto a Specific Branch
article_steps.content: Rebase a branch onto a different base:
article_steps.command:
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
# Replays feature-b commits that are not in feature-a onto main

article_steps.title: What is Interactive Rebase?
article_steps.content: Interactive rebase opens an editor showing your recent commits and lets you choose what to do with each one: keep, edit, squash, reorder, or drop. It is the most powerful tool for cleaning up your commit history.

article_steps.title: Start an Interactive Rebase
article_steps.content: Rebase the last N commits interactively:
article_steps.command:
# Edit the last 4 commits:
git rebase -i HEAD~4

article_steps.title: Understanding the Commands
article_steps.content:
In the editor, each line shows a commit with a command prefix:

pick = use the commit as-is
reword = use the commit but edit the message
edit = pause at this commit to amend it
squash = combine with previous commit (keep both messages)
fixup = combine with previous commit (discard this message)
drop = remove the commit entirely

article_steps.title: Squash Commits Together
article_steps.content: Combine multiple commits into one clean commit. Change 'pick' to 'squash' for the commits you want to fold in:
article_steps.command:
# In the editor, change:
pick abc1234 Add login form
pick def5678 Fix typo in login
pick ghi9012 Update login styles

# To:
pick abc1234 Add login form
squash def5678 Fix typo in login
squash ghi9012 Update login styles

article_steps.title: Reorder Commits
article_steps.content: Simply rearrange the lines in the editor to change the order of commits. Be careful — reordering can cause conflicts if commits depend on each other.

article_steps.title: Abort if Something Goes Wrong
article_steps.content: If the rebase gets complicated, you can always abort:
article_steps.command:
git rebase --abort
# Returns everything to the state before the rebase

article_steps.title: Why Protect Branches?
article_steps.content: Branch protection rules prevent accidental or unauthorized changes to critical branches like main or production. They enforce best practices like code review and passing tests before changes can be merged.

article_steps.title: Common Protection Rules
article_steps.content:
Popular rules to enable:

1. Require pull request reviews before merging
2. Require status checks to pass (CI/CD tests)
3. Prevent force pushes
4. Prevent branch deletion
5. Require signed commits
6. Require linear history (no merge commits)

article_steps.title: Set Up on GitHub
article_steps.content: Go to your repository → Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule. Enter 'main' as the branch name pattern, then select the rules you want to enforce.

article_steps.title: What Happens When Rules Are Active
article_steps.content:
When protection is enabled:
- Direct pushes to the protected branch are rejected
- Merges require approved pull requests
- Force pushes are blocked
- The branch cannot be deleted

Admins can optionally bypass these rules.

article_steps.title: Working with Protected Branches
article_steps.content: The standard workflow with protected branches:
article_steps.command:
# Create a feature branch:
git switch -c feature/new-feature

# Make changes and push:
git push -u origin feature/new-feature

# Then create a Pull Request on GitHub for review

article_steps.title: What is Gitflow?
article_steps.content: Gitflow is a branching model designed by Vincent Driessen. It defines a strict branching structure with specific roles for different branch types. It works well for projects with scheduled release cycles.

article_steps.title: Branch Types in Gitflow
article_steps.content:
main – always contains production-ready code
develop – integration branch for features
feature/* – individual feature development
release/* – preparing a new production release
hotfix/* – urgent fixes for production bugs

article_steps.title: Feature Development
article_steps.content: Create feature branches from develop:
article_steps.command:
git switch develop
git switch -c feature/shopping-cart

# Work on the feature, then merge back:
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feature/shopping-cart
git branch -d feature/shopping-cart

article_steps.title: Release Process
article_steps.content: When develop has enough features for a release:
article_steps.command:
git switch develop
git switch -c release/1.2.0

# Fix bugs, update version numbers, then:
git switch main
git merge --no-ff release/1.2.0
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"

# Also merge back into develop:
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff release/1.2.0
git branch -d release/1.2.0

article_steps.title: Hotfix Process
article_steps.content: For urgent production fixes:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git switch -c hotfix/fix-payment-bug

# Fix the bug, then merge into both main and develop:
git switch main
git merge --no-ff hotfix/fix-payment-bug
git tag -a v1.2.1 -m "Hotfix 1.2.1"

git switch develop
git merge --no-ff hotfix/fix-payment-bug
git branch -d hotfix/fix-payment-bug

article_steps.title: Rename the Current Branch
article_steps.content: If you are already on the branch you want to rename:
article_steps.command: git branch -m new-name

article_steps.title: Rename a Different Branch
article_steps.content: Rename a branch you are NOT currently on:
article_steps.command: git branch -m old-name new-name

article_steps.title: Update the Remote
article_steps.content: After renaming locally, update the remote by deleting the old name and pushing the new one:
article_steps.command:
# Delete the old remote branch:
git push origin --delete old-name

# Push the renamed branch:
git push -u origin new-name

article_steps.title: Notify Your Team
article_steps.content: Other developers will need to update their local references. They should run:
article_steps.command:
git fetch --all --prune
git switch new-name

article_steps.title: What is a Tracking Branch?
article_steps.content: A tracking branch is a local branch that has a direct relationship to a remote branch. When you clone a repository, your local 'main' automatically tracks 'origin/main'. This lets you use git push and git pull without specifying the remote each time.

article_steps.title: View Tracking Relationships
article_steps.content: See which local branches track which remote branches:
article_steps.command:
git branch -vv
# Output shows: branch hash [upstream] message

article_steps.title: Set Up Tracking
article_steps.content: Link a local branch to a remote branch:
article_steps.command:
# When pushing a new branch for the first time:
git push -u origin feature-branch

# Or set tracking explicitly:
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/feature-branch feature-branch

article_steps.title: Change Tracking Branch
article_steps.content: Point your local branch to a different remote branch:
article_steps.command: git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/new-remote-branch

article_steps.title: Check Ahead/Behind Status
article_steps.content: After setting tracking, git status tells you how many commits ahead or behind you are:
article_steps.command:
git status
# Output: Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 3 commits

article_steps.title: What are Long-Lived Branches?
article_steps.content: Long-lived branches exist alongside main for extended periods. Common examples include 'develop', 'staging', and 'production'. Unlike feature branches that are merged and deleted, these branches persist throughout the project lifecycle.

article_steps.title: Keep Them in Sync
article_steps.content: Regularly merge main into long-lived branches to prevent massive drift:
article_steps.command:
git switch develop
git merge main
# Resolve any conflicts and commit

article_steps.title: Common Long-Lived Branch Setup
article_steps.content:
A typical setup:

main → production-ready code (deployed to production)
staging → pre-production testing (deployed to staging server)
develop → active development (deployed to dev server)

Code flows: feature → develop → staging → main

article_steps.title: Avoid Divergence
article_steps.content:
The longer a branch lives without syncing, the harder merges become. Best practices:

1. Merge or rebase from main at least weekly
2. Keep the number of long-lived branches minimal
3. Use CI/CD to test each branch independently
4. Never let branches diverge for more than a sprint

article_steps.title: Promoting Changes Between Branches
article_steps.content: Move code through your branch hierarchy:
article_steps.command:
# Feature complete, merge into develop:
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feature/new-api

# Ready for testing, merge into staging:
git switch staging
git merge develop

# Tested and approved, merge into main:
git switch main
git merge staging
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Release 2.0"

article_steps.title: Why Compare Branches?
article_steps.content: Before merging, it is helpful to see exactly what changes a branch introduces. This helps you anticipate merge conflicts and review the scope of changes.

article_steps.title: See All Differences
article_steps.content: Compare the full diff between two branches:
article_steps.command: git diff main..feature-branch

article_steps.title: See Only Changed File Names
article_steps.content: Get a quick overview of which files were modified:
article_steps.command:
git diff --name-only main..feature-branch
# Or with status indicators (A/M/D):
git diff --name-status main..feature-branch

article_steps.title: See Commits Unique to a Branch
article_steps.content: List commits that exist in feature but not in main:
article_steps.command: git log main..feature-branch --oneline

article_steps.title: Statistical Summary
article_steps.content: Get a summary of additions and deletions per file:
article_steps.command: git diff --stat main..feature-branch

article_steps.title: How It Works
article_steps.content: In the Feature Branch workflow, no work happens directly on main. Every new feature, bug fix, or improvement gets its own branch. When the work is complete, it is merged back into main through a pull request.

article_steps.title: Step 1: Create a Feature Branch
article_steps.content: Start from an up-to-date main branch:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feature/user-profile

article_steps.title: Step 2: Work and Commit
article_steps.content: Make changes on your feature branch with regular commits:
article_steps.command:
# Make changes...
git add .
git commit -m "Add user profile page layout"

# Continue working...
git add .
git commit -m "Add profile photo upload"

article_steps.title: Step 3: Push and Create Pull Request
article_steps.content: Push your branch and open a pull request for review:
article_steps.command:
git push -u origin feature/user-profile
# Go to GitHub and create a Pull Request

article_steps.title: Step 4: Review, Merge, and Clean Up
article_steps.content: After the pull request is approved and merged:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Delete the feature branch:
git branch -d feature/user-profile
git push origin --delete feature/user-profile

article_steps.title: What is a Release Branch?
article_steps.content: A release branch is created when you want to prepare a new production release. It allows the team to stabilize the release (fix bugs, update docs) while other developers continue working on new features in develop.

article_steps.title: Create a Release Branch
article_steps.content: Branch off from develop when features are complete:
article_steps.command:
git switch develop
git switch -c release/2.0.0

article_steps.title: Stabilize the Release
article_steps.content:
On the release branch, only fix bugs and update version numbers. No new features.

Typical activities:
- Fix bugs found during QA testing
- Update version numbers in package.json
- Update changelog and documentation
- Final performance testing

article_steps.title: Finish the Release
article_steps.content: Merge into main and tag, then merge back into develop:
article_steps.command:
# Merge into main:
git switch main
git merge --no-ff release/2.0.0
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Release 2.0.0"
git push origin main --tags

# Merge back into develop:
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff release/2.0.0
git push origin develop

# Delete the release branch:
git branch -d release/2.0.0

article_steps.title: When to Use Release Branches
article_steps.content:
Release branches are valuable when:
- Multiple features need to be bundled into a release
- QA testing takes time
- You need to support multiple production versions
- You want a clear separation between development and release preparation

article_steps.title: The Core Difference
article_steps.content:
Merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit. It preserves the exact history.

Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch. It creates a linear history as if you worked sequentially.

article_steps.title: When to Use Merge
article_steps.content:
Use merge when:
- Working on shared branches (main, develop)
- You want to preserve the complete history
- Multiple people are working on the same branch
- You want a clear record of when features were integrated
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git merge feature-branch

article_steps.title: When to Use Rebase
article_steps.content:
Use rebase when:
- Cleaning up local commits before a pull request
- You want a clean, linear history
- Pulling upstream changes into your feature branch
- Your commits have not been pushed yet
article_steps.command:
git switch feature-branch
git rebase main

article_steps.title: The Danger of Rebase
article_steps.content: WARNING: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote branch. Rebase rewrites commit hashes, which causes divergence for anyone who has copies of those commits.

article_steps.title: A Practical Compromise
article_steps.content:
Many teams use this approach:
1. Rebase your feature branch on main before creating a PR (clean history)
2. Use merge (or squash merge) to merge the PR into main (preserve integration points)

This gives you the best of both worlds: clean feature history and clear merge points.

article_steps.title: What is a Three-Way Merge?
article_steps.content:
A three-way merge uses three reference points to combine changes:
1. The common ancestor commit (merge base)
2. The tip of your current branch
3. The tip of the branch being merged

Git compares both branches against the ancestor to determine what changed on each side.

article_steps.title: Find the Merge Base
article_steps.content: See the common ancestor of two branches:
article_steps.command: git merge-base main feature-branch

article_steps.title: How It Resolves Changes
article_steps.content:
For each part of a file, Git checks:
- Only branch A changed it → use branch A's version
- Only branch B changed it → use branch B's version
- Neither branch changed it → keep the ancestor's version
- Both branches changed it the same way → use either (they agree)
- Both branches changed it differently → CONFLICT (manual resolution needed)

article_steps.title: When Three-Way Merge Happens
article_steps.content: A three-way merge occurs when both branches have new commits since they diverged. If only one branch has new commits, Git does a fast-forward merge instead.
article_steps.command:
# This creates a merge commit (three-way merge):
git switch main
git merge feature-branch
# If both main and feature-branch have new commits

article_steps.title: What is an Octopus Merge?
article_steps.content: An octopus merge combines three or more branches into one merge commit. Git uses the 'octopus' merge strategy automatically when you specify multiple branches. It is useful when integrating several independent feature branches at once.

article_steps.title: Perform an Octopus Merge
article_steps.content: Merge multiple branches at once:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git merge feature-a feature-b feature-c

article_steps.title: When to Use
article_steps.content:
Octopus merges work well when:
- Multiple independent features need to be integrated simultaneously
- The branches don't have conflicting changes
- You want a single merge point in history

They do NOT work when there are conflicts — Git will refuse and ask you to merge branches one at a time.

article_steps.title: Limitations
article_steps.content: The octopus strategy cannot resolve conflicts. If any two branches modify the same lines, the merge will fail. In practice, octopus merges are rare. Most teams merge branches one at a time through pull requests.

article_steps.title: Available Merge Strategies
article_steps.content:
Git offers several merge strategies:

- ort (default since Git 2.34, replaces recursive)
- recursive (previous default for two-branch merges)
- resolve (simpler alternative to recursive)
- octopus (for merging multiple branches)
- ours (keep our version, discard theirs)
- subtree (merge a subdirectory)

article_steps.title: Specifying a Strategy
article_steps.content: Choose a specific merge strategy:
article_steps.command:
git merge -s resolve feature-branch
# Or:
git merge -s ours feature-branch

article_steps.title: Strategy Options (ours/theirs)
article_steps.content: When using the default strategy, you can specify how conflicts should be resolved:
article_steps.command:
# Always prefer our changes on conflict:
git merge -X ours feature-branch

# Always prefer their changes on conflict:
git merge -X theirs feature-branch

article_steps.title: The 'ours' Strategy vs 'ours' Option
article_steps.content:
These are different things:

-s ours (strategy): Completely ignores the other branch's changes. The merge commit exists but the tree is identical to the current branch. Used to record a merge without taking changes.

-X ours (option): Uses the default strategy but prefers our side when conflicts arise. Non-conflicting changes from both sides are still merged.

article_steps.title: When to Change Strategy
article_steps.content:
Most of the time, the default strategy works perfectly. Change it only when:
- You need to discard an entire branch's changes (-s ours)
- You want automatic conflict resolution (-X theirs)
- You are merging many branches simultaneously (octopus)

article_steps.title: Why Binary Conflicts are Different
article_steps.content: Git cannot show line-by-line diffs for binary files (images, PDFs, compiled files). When both branches modify the same binary file, Git cannot merge them automatically. You must choose one version or the other.

article_steps.title: Identify Binary Conflicts
article_steps.content: Git will report the conflict:
article_steps.command:
git merge feature-branch
# Output: warning: Cannot merge binary files: logo.png

article_steps.title: Keep Our Version
article_steps.content: Keep the version from your current branch:
article_steps.command:
git checkout --ours -- path/to/logo.png
git add path/to/logo.png

article_steps.title: Keep Their Version
article_steps.content: Keep the version from the branch being merged:
article_steps.command:
git checkout --theirs -- path/to/logo.png
git add path/to/logo.png

article_steps.title: Complete the Merge
article_steps.content: After resolving all binary conflicts, commit:
article_steps.command: git commit -m "Resolved binary file conflicts"

article_steps.title: Why Use a Merge Tool?
article_steps.content: Resolving conflicts in a text editor with conflict markers can be confusing. Merge tools provide a visual side-by-side (or three-way) view showing the base, local, and remote versions, making it much easier to choose the right changes.

article_steps.title: Configure VS Code as Merge Tool
article_steps.content: Set VS Code as your default merge tool:
article_steps.command:
git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd "code --wait $MERGED"

article_steps.title: Configure Other Merge Tools
article_steps.content: Set up popular alternatives:
article_steps.command:
# Meld (cross-platform, free):
git config --global merge.tool meld

# KDiff3 (cross-platform, free):
git config --global merge.tool kdiff3

# Beyond Compare (commercial):
git config --global merge.tool bc3

article_steps.title: Launch the Merge Tool
article_steps.content: When you have conflicts, launch the configured tool:
article_steps.command:
git mergetool
# Git opens each conflicting file in your merge tool

article_steps.title: Clean Up After Merging
article_steps.content: Merge tools create .orig backup files. Clean them up:
article_steps.command:
# Remove .orig files:
find . -name "*.orig" -delete

# Or prevent them from being created:
git config --global mergetool.keepBackup false

article_steps.title: The Resolve Strategy
article_steps.content: The resolve strategy is the simplest three-way merge. It finds a single common ancestor (merge base) and performs a straightforward three-way merge. It works well when there is only one merge base.

article_steps.title: The Recursive Strategy
article_steps.content: The recursive strategy handles cases where there are multiple common ancestors (criss-cross merges). It creates a temporary virtual merge base by merging the common ancestors first, then uses that as the base for the final merge.

article_steps.title: When Multiple Merge Bases Exist
article_steps.content: Criss-cross merges happen when two branches have been merged into each other in both directions. The recursive strategy handles this correctly by recursively merging the bases. The resolve strategy picks one arbitrarily.

article_steps.title: Using Each Strategy
article_steps.content: Specify the strategy explicitly:
article_steps.command:
# Recursive (was default before Git 2.34):
git merge -s recursive feature-branch

# Resolve (simpler, sometimes faster):
git merge -s resolve feature-branch

# ORT (current default, successor to recursive):
git merge -s ort feature-branch

article_steps.title: Practical Advice
article_steps.content: In practice, you almost never need to specify a merge strategy. The default (ort/recursive) handles 99.9% of cases correctly. Only consider alternatives if you encounter unusual merge problems or need specific behavior.

article_steps.title: Assess the Scope
article_steps.content: Before diving in, understand the scale of the conflict:
article_steps.command:
# See how many files have conflicts:
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U

# Count conflicting files:
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U | wc -l

article_steps.title: Resolve File by File
article_steps.content:
Work through conflicts systematically:

1. Start with the simplest files (fewer conflict markers)
2. Use a merge tool for visual comparison
3. Test after resolving each critical file
4. Stage resolved files as you go
article_steps.command:
# Check remaining unresolved files:
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U

# After resolving a file:
git add resolved-file.js

article_steps.title: Use ours/theirs for Bulk Resolution
article_steps.content: If you know one side is correct for entire files:
article_steps.command:
# Accept our version for specific files:
git checkout --ours -- src/generated/*.js
git add src/generated/

# Accept their version for specific files:
git checkout --theirs -- config/*.json
git add config/

article_steps.title: Take Breaks and Test
article_steps.content:
For massive conflicts:

1. Resolve conflicts in logical groups (by feature or directory)
2. Run tests after each group
3. Commit partial progress if possible
4. Don't try to resolve everything in one sitting

article_steps.title: Prevention is Better
article_steps.content:
To avoid large merge conflicts in the future:

1. Merge main into your branch frequently
2. Keep feature branches small and short-lived
3. Coordinate with teammates on shared files
4. Use feature flags instead of long-lived branches
5. Do regular code reviews to catch divergence early

article_steps.title: 1. Update Your Branches
article_steps.content: Make sure both branches are up to date with the remote:
article_steps.command:
git fetch origin
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch feature-branch
git pull origin feature-branch

article_steps.title: 2. Review the Changes
article_steps.content: Inspect what will be merged:
article_steps.command:
# See changed files:
git diff --name-only main..feature-branch

# See the full diff:
git diff main..feature-branch

# See commit list:
git log main..feature-branch --oneline

article_steps.title: 3. Run Tests
article_steps.content: Before merging, ensure all tests pass on both branches. Run your project's test suite on the feature branch to catch any issues before they reach main.

article_steps.title: 4. Check for Conflicts
article_steps.content: Do a dry run to check for conflicts without actually merging:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git merge --no-commit --no-ff feature-branch
# Check the result, then abort:
git merge --abort

article_steps.title: 5. Merge with Confidence
article_steps.content: After verifying everything, perform the merge:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature-branch -m "Merge feature-branch: Add user authentication"

article_steps.title: Why Merge Commits Matter
article_steps.content: Merge commits mark integration points in your history. A good merge commit message explains what was merged and why, making it easy to understand the project timeline later.

article_steps.title: Write a Good Merge Message
article_steps.content: Include the purpose, not just the branch name:
article_steps.command:
# Bad:
git merge feature-branch

# Good:
git merge --no-ff feature-branch -m "Merge 'feature-branch': Add OAuth2 login with Google and GitHub providers"

article_steps.title: Merge Commit Format
article_steps.content:
A clear format for merge messages:

Merge 'branch-name': Brief summary of what was added

Optional body with:
- Key features or changes introduced
- Any breaking changes
- Related issue numbers

article_steps.title: Viewing Merge History
article_steps.content: Filter your log to show only merge commits:
article_steps.command:
git log --merges --oneline
# Shows only merge commits, making it easy to see integration points

article_steps.title: Squash Merge Alternative
article_steps.content: If you prefer a single clean commit instead of a merge commit:
article_steps.command:
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "Add OAuth2 login with Google and GitHub providers"
# Creates a single commit with all the branch's changes

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Issues?
article_steps.content: Issues are GitHub's built-in project tracking tool. They can represent bugs, feature requests, tasks, or any work item. Each issue gets a unique number and can be labeled, assigned, and linked to pull requests.

article_steps.title: Create an Issue
article_steps.content:
Click 'New Issue' on the Issues tab. Include:

1. Clear, descriptive title
2. Steps to reproduce (for bugs)
3. Expected vs actual behavior
4. Screenshots if applicable
5. Environment details (OS, browser, version)

article_steps.title: Using Labels
article_steps.content:
Labels categorize issues:

bug – something is broken
enhancement – new feature request
documentation – docs need updating
good first issue – beginner-friendly task
help wanted – looking for contributors
priority: high – needs immediate attention

article_steps.title: Reference Issues in Commits
article_steps.content: Link commits to issues by including the issue number:
article_steps.command: git commit -m "Fix login timeout error (fixes #42)"

article_steps.title: Close Issues Automatically
article_steps.content:
Using keywords in commit messages or PR descriptions automatically closes issues when merged:

Keywords: fixes, closes, resolves

Example: 'This PR resolves #42 and fixes #55'

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Actions?
article_steps.content: GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform built into GitHub. It lets you create automated workflows that run when events happen in your repository (push, pull request, schedule). Workflows are defined in YAML files.

article_steps.title: Create Your First Workflow
article_steps.content: Create a workflow file in your repository:
article_steps.command:
mkdir -p .github/workflows
# Create .github/workflows/ci.yml

article_steps.title: Basic CI Workflow Example
article_steps.content:
A simple workflow that runs tests on every push:

name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test

article_steps.title: Key Concepts
article_steps.content:
Workflow: Automated process defined in YAML
Event: Trigger that starts a workflow (push, PR, schedule)
Job: Set of steps that run on the same runner
Step: Individual task (run a script or use an action)
Action: Reusable component from the GitHub Marketplace
Runner: Server that runs the workflow (ubuntu, windows, macos)

article_steps.title: Trigger on Pull Requests Only
article_steps.content:
Run workflows only on pull requests to specific branches:

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

This saves CI minutes by only running when PRs target important branches.

article_steps.title: View Workflow Results
article_steps.content: Go to the Actions tab in your repository to see workflow runs. Each run shows the status (success/failure), logs, and which commit triggered it.

article_steps.title: What is GitHub Pages?
article_steps.content: GitHub Pages is a free static site hosting service that serves HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files directly from a GitHub repository. It is perfect for personal websites, project documentation, and portfolios.

article_steps.title: Enable GitHub Pages
article_steps.content: Go to your repository → Settings → Pages. Select the source branch (usually 'main') and the folder (root or /docs). Click Save.

article_steps.title: Create Your Site
article_steps.content: Add an index.html file to your repository:
article_steps.command:
echo 'My Site

Hello World

' > index.html git add index.html git commit -m "Add GitHub Pages site" git push

article_steps.title: Access Your Site
article_steps.content:
Your site will be available at:
https://username.github.io/repository-name/

It may take a few minutes for the first deployment to complete.

article_steps.title: Custom Domain
article_steps.content:
You can use a custom domain instead of the github.io URL:

1. Add a CNAME file to your repo containing your domain name
2. Configure DNS records with your domain provider to point to GitHub's servers
3. Enable 'Enforce HTTPS' in repository settings

article_steps.title: Why Use PR Templates?
article_steps.content: PR templates pre-fill the description when someone opens a new pull request. They ensure contributors provide the right information: what changed, why, how to test it, and any related issues.

article_steps.title: Create a Template
article_steps.content: Create a pull request template file:
article_steps.command:
# Option 1: Root directory
touch PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md

# Option 2: .github directory (cleaner)
mkdir -p .github
touch .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md

article_steps.title: Template Content Example
article_steps.content:
A practical template:

## Description
Brief description of what this PR does.

## Type of Change
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update

## How Has This Been Tested?
Describe the tests you ran.

## Checklist
- [ ] My code follows the project's style guidelines
- [ ] I have performed a self-review
- [ ] I have added tests for my changes
- [ ] All new and existing tests pass

## Related Issues
Closes #(issue number)

article_steps.title: Commit and Push
article_steps.content: Add the template to your repository:
article_steps.command:
git add .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
git commit -m "Add pull request template"
git push

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Releases?
article_steps.content: Releases are GitHub's way of packaging software versions. They combine Git tags with release notes, binary downloads, and changelogs. Users can download specific versions of your software from the Releases page.

article_steps.title: Create a Tag First
article_steps.content: Releases are based on Git tags:
article_steps.command:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"
git push origin v1.0.0

article_steps.title: Create a Release on GitHub
article_steps.content:
Go to your repository → Releases → Draft a new release:

1. Choose the tag you created
2. Set the release title (e.g., 'v1.0.0 – Initial Release')
3. Write release notes describing changes
4. Upload binary assets if applicable
5. Mark as pre-release if not production-ready
6. Click 'Publish release'

article_steps.title: Write Good Release Notes
article_steps.content:
Structure your release notes:

## What's New
- Feature A: Brief description
- Feature B: Brief description

## Bug Fixes
- Fixed issue #42: Description

## Breaking Changes
- API endpoint changed from /v1 to /v2

## Contributors
@username1, @username2

article_steps.title: Auto-Generate Release Notes
article_steps.content: GitHub can auto-generate notes from merged PRs. Click 'Generate release notes' when creating a release. It lists all PRs merged since the last release, grouped by label.

article_steps.title: What is GitHub CLI?
article_steps.content: GitHub CLI (gh) is an official command-line tool for GitHub. It lets you create repos, manage issues, review PRs, and run Actions — all from your terminal without opening a browser.

article_steps.title: Install and Authenticate
article_steps.content: Install GitHub CLI and log in:
article_steps.command:
# Install (varies by OS):
# Mac: brew install gh
# Windows: winget install GitHub.cli
# Linux: See cli.github.com for instructions

# Authenticate:
gh auth login

article_steps.title: Work with Repositories
article_steps.content: Common repository operations:
article_steps.command:
# Create a new repo:
gh repo create my-project --public

# Clone a repo:
gh repo clone username/repo-name

# View repo in browser:
gh repo view --web

article_steps.title: Work with Pull Requests
article_steps.content: Manage PRs from the terminal:
article_steps.command:
# Create a PR:
gh pr create --title "Add login feature" --body "Implements user login"

# List open PRs:
gh pr list

# Checkout a PR locally:
gh pr checkout 42

# Merge a PR:
gh pr merge 42

article_steps.title: Work with Issues
article_steps.content: Manage issues from the terminal:
article_steps.command:
# Create an issue:
gh issue create --title "Bug: Login fails" --body "Steps to reproduce..."

# List open issues:
gh issue list

# Close an issue:
gh issue close 42

article_steps.title: What are Codespaces?
article_steps.content: GitHub Codespaces provides cloud-hosted development environments. You get a full VS Code editor running in the cloud with your repository pre-loaded. No local setup needed — everything runs in a container.

article_steps.title: Create a Codespace
article_steps.content: From any repository on GitHub, click the green 'Code' button, then the 'Codespaces' tab, and click 'Create codespace on main'. VS Code opens in your browser with the project ready.

article_steps.title: Configure with devcontainer.json
article_steps.content:
Customize your codespace environment by adding a configuration file:

.devcontainer/devcontainer.json:
{
  "name": "My Project",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/javascript-node:20",
  "postCreateCommand": "npm install",
  "forwardPorts": [3000]
}

article_steps.title: Using the Terminal
article_steps.content: Codespaces include a full Linux terminal. Use it like any development machine:
article_steps.command:
# All tools are available:
npm install
npm run dev
git commit -m "Made changes in codespace"

article_steps.title: Manage Codespaces
article_steps.content: View and manage your codespaces from the command line:
article_steps.command:
# List your codespaces:
gh codespace list

# Stop a running codespace:
gh codespace stop

# Delete a codespace:
gh codespace delete

article_steps.title: How Notifications Work
article_steps.content:
GitHub sends notifications when:
- You are mentioned (@username)
- You are assigned to an issue or PR
- You are a reviewer on a PR
- You are watching a repository
- A thread you participated in is updated

article_steps.title: Watch Settings
article_steps.content:
For each repository, choose your notification level:

All Activity – every event (very noisy)
Participating and @mentions – only when you are involved (recommended)
Ignore – no notifications from this repo
Custom – choose specific event types

article_steps.title: Filter Your Inbox
article_steps.content:
Use the notification inbox at github.com/notifications to:

1. Filter by reason (assigned, mentioned, review requested)
2. Filter by repository
3. Mark as read/unread
4. Save important notifications for later
5. Unsubscribe from threads you don't need

article_steps.title: Email Notifications
article_steps.content:
Configure email preferences at Settings → Notifications. You can:
- Receive email for all notifications or only participating
- Route different repos to different email addresses
- Disable email entirely and use only the web inbox

article_steps.title: What is a Template Repository?
article_steps.content: A template repository serves as a blueprint for new projects. Unlike forking, using a template creates a fresh repository with no Git history. It includes your pre-configured files, directory structure, and documentation.

article_steps.title: Create a Template
article_steps.content:
Set up your template repository:

1. Create a new repository with your standard files
2. Add common configurations (CI/CD, linting, .gitignore)
3. Go to Settings → check 'Template repository'
4. The repo now shows a 'Use this template' button

article_steps.title: Use a Template
article_steps.content:
Create a new repository from a template:

1. Go to the template repository on GitHub
2. Click 'Use this template' → 'Create a new repository'
3. Name your new repo and click 'Create repository'
4. Clone and start coding — no inherited history

article_steps.title: Use Templates from CLI
article_steps.content: Create a repo from a template using GitHub CLI:
article_steps.command: gh repo create my-new-project --template username/template-repo --public --clone

article_steps.title: What to Include in Templates
article_steps.content:
Good template contents:
- README.md with setup instructions
- .gitignore for the tech stack
- CI/CD workflow files (.github/workflows/)
- Linter configurations (.eslintrc, .prettierrc)
- PR and issue templates
- LICENSE file
- Basic project structure (src/, tests/, docs/)

article_steps.title: Why Code Review Matters
article_steps.content: Code reviews catch bugs, improve code quality, share knowledge across the team, and ensure consistency. Studies show that code review is one of the most effective ways to find and prevent defects.

article_steps.title: Reviewing a Pull Request
article_steps.content:
When reviewing a PR on GitHub:

1. Read the PR description and linked issues
2. Go to the 'Files changed' tab
3. Review each file's changes
4. Click the '+' icon next to a line to add a comment
5. Submit your review as 'Approve', 'Request Changes', or 'Comment'

article_steps.title: Writing Good Review Comments
article_steps.content:
Effective review comments:

- Be specific: Point to the exact line and explain the issue
- Be constructive: Suggest solutions, not just problems
- Be kind: Use 'nit:' for minor suggestions, 'suggestion:' for improvements
- Ask questions when unsure: 'Is this intentional?'
- Praise good code: Positive feedback encourages best practices

article_steps.title: Using Suggested Changes
article_steps.content: GitHub lets you suggest specific code changes inline. Click the file diff icon when commenting and edit the code. The PR author can accept your suggestion with one click.

article_steps.title: Review from the CLI
article_steps.content: Review PRs from your terminal:
article_steps.command:
# View PR diff:
gh pr diff 42

# Approve a PR:
gh pr review 42 --approve

# Request changes:
gh pr review 42 --request-changes --body "Please fix the SQL injection vulnerability"

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Secrets?
