article_steps.content: Secrets are encrypted environment variables stored in your GitHub repository. They are used in GitHub Actions workflows to safely access sensitive data like API keys, database passwords, and deployment credentials without exposing them in code.

article_steps.title: Add a Secret
article_steps.content: Go to repository Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret. Enter a name (e.g., API_KEY) and the value. Secrets are encrypted and cannot be viewed after saving.

article_steps.title: Use Secrets in Workflows
article_steps.content:
Reference secrets in your GitHub Actions workflow:

steps:
  - name: Deploy
    env:
      API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
    run: npm run deploy

article_steps.title: Set Secrets via CLI
article_steps.content: Add secrets from your terminal:
article_steps.command:
# Set a secret:
gh secret set API_KEY --body "your-secret-value"

# Set from a file:
gh secret set DEPLOY_KEY < deploy_key.pem

# List secrets:
gh secret list

article_steps.title: Security Notes
article_steps.content:
Important security practices:

- Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered by forks (prevents secret theft)
- Secrets are masked in workflow logs (replaced with ***)
- Use environment-specific secrets for staging vs production
- Rotate secrets regularly
- Never hardcode secrets in your repository files

article_steps.title: Why Protect Branches?
article_steps.content: Protected branches prevent accidental or unauthorized changes to critical branches like main. They enforce team workflows by requiring reviews and passing tests before code can be merged.

article_steps.title: Set Up Protection
article_steps.content:
Go to Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule:

1. Enter the branch name pattern (e.g., 'main')
2. Select your desired rules
3. Click 'Create' to save

article_steps.title: Key Protection Options
article_steps.content:
Require a pull request before merging – no direct pushes
Require approvals – specify minimum number of reviewers
Dismiss stale reviews – require re-review after new commits
Require status checks – CI must pass before merging
Require branches to be up to date – must be current with base
Restrict who can push – limit to specific people or teams
Block force pushes – prevent history rewriting
Require linear history – no merge commits (rebase only)

article_steps.title: Rulesets (Newer Feature)
article_steps.content: GitHub Rulesets are a newer, more flexible alternative to branch protection rules. They can target multiple branches, be applied at the organization level, and include additional rule types. Find them under Settings → Rules → Rulesets.

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Discussions?
article_steps.content: Discussions provide a forum-like space within your repository for conversations that don't fit into Issues or PRs. They are threaded, categorized, and searchable — ideal for Q&A, announcements, and brainstorming.

article_steps.title: Enable Discussions
article_steps.content: Go to Settings → Features → check 'Discussions'. A new Discussions tab appears in your repository.

article_steps.title: Discussion Categories
article_steps.content:
Default categories include:

Announcements – project news and updates
General – open-ended conversations
Ideas – feature suggestions and brainstorming
Polls – community voting
Q&A – questions with accepted answers
Show and tell – share projects and achievements

article_steps.title: Best Practices
article_steps.content:
Use Discussions for:
- Design decisions and RFC (Request for Comments)
- Q&A where the community can help
- Announcements about releases and changes
- Gathering feedback on proposed features

Use Issues for:
- Actionable bug reports
- Specific feature requests
- Tasks that need to be tracked and closed

article_steps.title: What are GitHub Projects?
article_steps.content: GitHub Projects (v2) is a flexible project management tool integrated with your repositories. It provides spreadsheet-like tables, Kanban boards, and timeline views to organize issues, PRs, and custom items.

article_steps.title: Create a Project
article_steps.content:
Go to your profile or organization → Projects → New project. Choose a template:

- Board: Kanban-style columns
- Table: Spreadsheet-style rows
- Roadmap: Timeline view
- Blank: Start from scratch

article_steps.title: Add Items
article_steps.content:
Add items to your project:

1. Convert existing Issues and PRs into project items
2. Create new draft items directly in the project
3. Items automatically inherit fields from their linked issues

article_steps.title: Custom Fields
article_steps.content:
Add custom fields to track additional data:

- Status: Todo, In Progress, Done
- Priority: High, Medium, Low
- Sprint: Sprint 1, Sprint 2
- Estimate: Story points or hours
- Custom text, number, or date fields

article_steps.title: Automate Your Board
article_steps.content:
Set up automations:

- When an issue is opened → set status to 'Todo'
- When a PR is merged → set status to 'Done'
- When an item is added → set default fields

Configure these under Project Settings → Workflows.

article_steps.title: Why Sign Commits?
article_steps.content: Anyone can set any name and email in git config. Commit signing uses GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) cryptography to prove that a commit actually came from you. GitHub shows a 'Verified' badge next to signed commits.

article_steps.title: Generate a GPG Key
article_steps.content: Create a new GPG key pair:
article_steps.command:
gpg --full-generate-key
# Choose RSA and RSA, 4096 bits, no expiration (or set one)
# Enter your name and the email associated with your GitHub account

article_steps.title: Find Your Key ID
article_steps.content: List your GPG keys and note the key ID:
article_steps.command:
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
# The key ID is the string after 'sec rsa4096/' (e.g., 3AA5C34371567BD2)

article_steps.title: Configure Git to Sign
article_steps.content: Tell Git to use your GPG key:
article_steps.command:
git config --global user.signingkey 3AA5C34371567BD2

# Sign all commits by default:
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

article_steps.title: Add GPG Key to GitHub
article_steps.content: Export your public key and add it to GitHub:
article_steps.command:
gpg --armor --export 3AA5C34371567BD2
# Copy the output (including BEGIN/END lines)
# Go to GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New GPG key → paste

article_steps.title: Sign a Commit
article_steps.content: Create a signed commit:
article_steps.command:
git commit -S -m "This commit is signed"

# Verify signatures on existing commits:
git log --show-signature

article_steps.title: What is Git Credential Manager?
article_steps.content: Git Credential Manager (GCM) securely stores your Git credentials (passwords, tokens) so you don't have to enter them every time. It uses your operating system's secure storage (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service).

article_steps.title: Install GCM
article_steps.content: GCM comes bundled with Git for Windows. On other platforms:
article_steps.command:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install git-credential-manager

# Linux:
# Download from github.com/git-ecosystem/git-credential-manager/releases
# Then configure:
git-credential-manager configure

article_steps.title: Verify It is Working
article_steps.content: Check that GCM is configured:
article_steps.command:
git config --global credential.helper
# Should output: manager-core (or manager)

article_steps.title: Clear Stored Credentials
article_steps.content: If you need to re-authenticate (e.g., after changing your token):
article_steps.command:
# Remove credentials for a specific host:
git credential-manager erase
protocol=https
host=github.com
# Press Enter twice

# Or use the OS credential manager directly

article_steps.title: Alternative: Simple Credential Cache
article_steps.content: If you prefer a lighter solution, cache credentials temporarily:
article_steps.command:
# Cache credentials in memory for 1 hour:
git config --global credential.helper 'cache --timeout=3600'

article_steps.title: Why Enable 2FA?
article_steps.content: Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security to your GitHub account. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot access your account without the second factor (your phone or security key). GitHub now requires 2FA for all contributors to public repositories.

article_steps.title: Set Up 2FA
article_steps.content:
Go to Settings → Password and authentication → Enable two-factor authentication.

Choose your method:
1. Authenticator app (recommended) – Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password
2. SMS text message (less secure)
3. Security key (hardware key like YubiKey)

article_steps.title: Save Recovery Codes
article_steps.content:
GitHub gives you recovery codes during setup. These are one-time codes you can use if you lose your 2FA device. Store them securely:

1. Save in a password manager
2. Print and store in a safe place
3. Do NOT put them in your repository

article_steps.title: Git Access with 2FA
article_steps.content:
After enabling 2FA, you CANNOT use your GitHub password for Git operations. You must use:

1. Personal Access Token (PAT) instead of password for HTTPS
2. SSH key authentication (recommended)
3. GitHub CLI (gh auth login)

article_steps.title: Verify 2FA is Active
article_steps.content: Go to Settings → Password and authentication. You should see 'Two-factor authentication' marked as enabled, with your configured methods listed.

article_steps.title: What are OAuth Apps?
article_steps.content: OAuth apps are third-party applications that request access to your GitHub account. When you 'Sign in with GitHub' on another website, that site is using OAuth to access your GitHub data with your permission.

article_steps.title: How OAuth Works
article_steps.content:
The flow:
1. App redirects you to GitHub
2. GitHub shows what permissions the app is requesting
3. You authorize (or deny) the request
4. GitHub sends the app a temporary access token
5. The app uses the token to access your data within the granted scope

article_steps.title: Understanding Scopes
article_steps.content:
Apps request specific permissions (scopes):

repo – full access to repositories
read:user – read your profile
user:email – access your email
workflow – manage GitHub Actions
delete_repo – delete repositories (dangerous!)

Only authorize apps that request reasonable scopes for their function.

article_steps.title: Review Authorized Apps
article_steps.content:
Check what apps have access to your account:

Go to Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps.

Review the list and revoke access for any apps you no longer use or trust.

article_steps.title: Revoke Access
article_steps.content:
To remove an app's access:

1. Go to Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps
2. Click the app name
3. Click 'Revoke access'

The app will immediately lose access to your GitHub data.

article_steps.title: The Challenge
article_steps.content: If you have both a personal and work GitHub account, Git needs to know which identity to use for each repository. This requires separate SSH keys and conditional Git configuration.

article_steps.title: Generate Separate SSH Keys
article_steps.content: Create a different key for each account:
article_steps.command:
# Personal account:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "personal@email.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_personal

# Work account:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "work@company.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work

article_steps.title: Configure SSH
article_steps.content: Create or edit ~/.ssh/config to map hosts to keys:
article_steps.command:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host github-personal
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_personal

Host github-work
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work

article_steps.title: Clone with the Right Identity
article_steps.content: Use the SSH host alias when cloning:
article_steps.command:
# Personal repo:
git clone git@github-personal:personal-user/repo.git

# Work repo:
git clone git@github-work:work-user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Conditional Git Config
article_steps.content: Set different name and email based on the directory:
article_steps.command:
# In ~/.gitconfig:
[user]
  name = Personal Name
  email = personal@email.com

[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
  path = ~/.gitconfig-work

# In ~/.gitconfig-work:
[user]
  name = Work Name
  email = work@company.com

article_steps.title: What are Deploy Keys?
article_steps.content: Deploy keys are SSH keys that grant access to a single repository. Unlike personal SSH keys (which access all your repos), deploy keys are scoped to one repo. They are ideal for servers and CI/CD systems that need repository access.

article_steps.title: Generate a Deploy Key
article_steps.content: Create an SSH key on your server:
article_steps.command:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "deploy-key-production" -f ~/.ssh/deploy_key
# Do NOT set a passphrase if using in automated systems

article_steps.title: Add to GitHub
article_steps.content:
Go to the repository → Settings → Deploy keys → Add deploy key:

1. Title: 'Production Server'
2. Key: paste the contents of deploy_key.pub
3. Allow write access: check only if the server needs to push
4. Click 'Add key'

article_steps.title: Use the Deploy Key
article_steps.content: Configure the server to use the deploy key:
article_steps.command:
# Clone using the deploy key:
GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key' git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git

# Or configure in ~/.ssh/config:
# Host github-deploy
#   HostName github.com
#   IdentityFile ~/.ssh/deploy_key

article_steps.title: Security Best Practices
article_steps.content:
1. Use read-only access unless write is truly needed
2. Each deploy key can only be used for ONE repository
3. Rotate deploy keys periodically
4. Remove deploy keys when servers are decommissioned
5. Never share deploy keys between servers

article_steps.title: Classic vs Fine-Grained Tokens
article_steps.content: Classic PATs have broad scopes (repo, user, etc.) that apply to ALL your repositories. Fine-grained tokens let you specify exact permissions for specific repositories, following the principle of least privilege.

article_steps.title: Create a Fine-Grained Token
article_steps.content:
Go to Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token:

1. Set a descriptive name
2. Set an expiration date (required)
3. Select 'Only select repositories' and choose specific repos
4. Under 'Permissions', enable only what you need
5. Click 'Generate token'

article_steps.title: Available Permission Categories
article_steps.content:
Fine-grained permissions include:

Repository permissions:
- Contents: read/write to repository files
- Issues: manage issues
- Pull requests: manage PRs
- Metadata: read-only repo info (always granted)

Account permissions:
- Email addresses: read your emails
- Followers: manage followers

article_steps.title: Use the Token
article_steps.content: Use the fine-grained token for HTTPS Git operations:
article_steps.command:
# Clone with token:
git clone https://oauth2:YOUR_TOKEN@github.com/user/repo.git

# Or update existing remote:
git remote set-url origin https://oauth2:YOUR_TOKEN@github.com/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Token Expiration
article_steps.content:
Fine-grained tokens require an expiration date (maximum 1 year). When a token expires:

1. Git operations using that token will fail
2. Go to Settings → Developer settings to regenerate
3. Update the token wherever it is used (servers, CI/CD)

article_steps.title: What is the Verified Badge?
article_steps.content: When you see a 'Verified' badge next to a commit on GitHub, it means the commit was cryptographically signed and GitHub confirmed the signature matches a key associated with the committer's account.

article_steps.title: Verification Statuses
article_steps.content:
GitHub shows three statuses:

Verified (green): Signature is valid and matches the committer's GitHub account
Partially Verified: Signed but the key is not linked to a GitHub account
Unverified: No signature, or the signature could not be verified

article_steps.title: Verify Commits Locally
article_steps.content: Check commit signatures from your terminal:
article_steps.command:
# Show signature for recent commits:
git log --show-signature -5

# Verify a specific commit:
git verify-commit abc1234

article_steps.title: SSH Signing (Modern Alternative)
article_steps.content: Since Git 2.34, you can sign commits with SSH keys instead of GPG:
article_steps.command:
# Configure SSH signing:
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

# Add the SSH key as a signing key on GitHub:
# Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type: Signing Key

article_steps.title: Vigilant Mode
article_steps.content: Enable vigilant mode in GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → check 'Flag unsigned commits as unverified'. This marks ALL your unsigned commits as 'Unverified', making it obvious when a commit claiming to be from you is not actually signed.

article_steps.title: Why Push to Multiple Remotes?
article_steps.content:
You might want to push to multiple remotes for:
- Backup: Mirror your code to GitHub and GitLab
- Migration: Gradually move from one platform to another
- CI/CD: Different remotes trigger different pipelines
- Open source: Maintain public and private copies

article_steps.title: Add Multiple Push URLs
article_steps.content: Add an additional push URL to your origin remote:
article_steps.command:
# Add a second push URL to origin:
git remote set-url --add --push origin https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git

# Verify:
git remote -v

article_steps.title: Add a Separate Remote
article_steps.content: Or add a completely separate remote:
article_steps.command:
git remote add gitlab https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git
git remote add bitbucket https://bitbucket.org/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Push to All Remotes
article_steps.content: Push to all remotes at once:
article_steps.command:
# Push to origin (includes all push URLs):
git push origin main

# Or push to specific remotes:
git push gitlab main
git push bitbucket main

article_steps.title: Create a Push-All Alias
article_steps.content: Create a convenient alias to push everywhere:
article_steps.command: git config --global alias.pushall '!git remote | xargs -I{} git push {} --all'

article_steps.title: What is a Bare Repository?
article_steps.content: A bare repository contains only the Git metadata (the contents of the .git directory) without a working directory. It is designed to be a central repository that developers push to and pull from. You never edit files directly in a bare repo.

article_steps.title: Create a Bare Repository
article_steps.content: Initialize a bare repository on your server:
article_steps.command:
git init --bare /path/to/project.git
# Convention: bare repos end with .git

article_steps.title: Clone from the Bare Repo
article_steps.content: Developers clone from the bare repo to get a working copy:
article_steps.command:
git clone user@server:/path/to/project.git
# Or over SSH:
git clone ssh://user@server/path/to/project.git

article_steps.title: Push to the Bare Repo
article_steps.content: Push changes to the central bare repository:
article_steps.command:
git remote add origin user@server:/path/to/project.git
git push -u origin main

article_steps.title: When to Use Bare Repos
article_steps.content:
Use bare repos when:
- Setting up a self-hosted Git server
- Creating a shared repository on a network drive
- Building a Git-based deployment system
- You need a central repo without GitHub/GitLab

Do NOT use bare repos for development work — they have no working directory.

article_steps.title: What is Mirroring?
article_steps.content: Mirroring creates an exact copy of a repository including all branches, tags, remote-tracking branches, and other refs. It is different from cloning, which only copies branches you check out.

article_steps.title: Create a Mirror
article_steps.content: Clone a repository as a mirror:
article_steps.command:
git clone --mirror https://github.com/original/repo.git
cd repo.git

article_steps.title: Push Mirror to Another Remote
article_steps.content: Push the mirror to a different hosting platform:
article_steps.command:
cd repo.git
git push --mirror https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Keep the Mirror Updated
article_steps.content: Regularly sync the mirror with the source:
article_steps.command:
cd repo.git
git remote update
git push --mirror https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Mirror vs Clone
article_steps.content:
Clone:
- Gets all branches but only checks out default
- Sets up origin remote for normal push/pull
- Used for development

Mirror:
- Gets ALL refs (branches, tags, remote refs, notes)
- Exact byte-for-byte copy of the source
- Used for backup, migration, or archival

article_steps.title: Why Use Shallow Clones?
article_steps.content: Large repositories with thousands of commits can take a long time to clone. Shallow clones download only recent history, dramatically reducing clone time and disk space. Partial clones download objects on demand.

article_steps.title: Shallow Clone
article_steps.content: Clone with limited history:
article_steps.command:
# Clone only the latest commit:
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/user/large-repo.git

# Clone the last 10 commits:
git clone --depth 10 https://github.com/user/large-repo.git

article_steps.title: Unshallow Later
article_steps.content: If you need the full history later, fetch it:
article_steps.command:
git fetch --unshallow
# Downloads all remaining history

article_steps.title: Partial Clone (Blobless)
article_steps.content: Clone without downloading file contents immediately:
article_steps.command:
# Blobless clone (downloads blobs on demand):
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/user/large-repo.git

# Treeless clone (downloads trees and blobs on demand):
git clone --filter=tree:0 https://github.com/user/large-repo.git

article_steps.title: Sparse Checkout
article_steps.content: Check out only specific directories from a large repo:
article_steps.command:
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/user/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout set src/frontend docs/
# Only src/frontend and docs/ are downloaded

article_steps.title: What are Submodules?
article_steps.content: Submodules let you include one Git repository inside another. The outer (parent) repo tracks a specific commit of the inner (submodule) repo. This is useful for shared libraries, vendor dependencies, or multi-repo projects.

article_steps.title: Add a Submodule
article_steps.content: Add an external repository as a submodule:
article_steps.command:
git submodule add https://github.com/user/shared-lib.git libs/shared-lib
git commit -m "Add shared-lib as submodule"

article_steps.title: Clone a Repo with Submodules
article_steps.content: When cloning a repo that uses submodules:
article_steps.command:
# Clone and initialize submodules in one command:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/user/project.git

# Or after cloning:
git submodule init
git submodule update

article_steps.title: Update Submodules
article_steps.content: Pull the latest changes in submodules:
article_steps.command:
# Update all submodules to their latest commits:
git submodule update --remote

# Then commit the updated references:
git add .
git commit -m "Update submodules to latest versions"

article_steps.title: Remove a Submodule
article_steps.content: Removing a submodule requires several steps:
article_steps.command:
# 1. Remove from .gitmodules and .git/config:
git submodule deinit -f libs/shared-lib

# 2. Remove from the working tree and index:
git rm -f libs/shared-lib

# 3. Remove the submodule's .git directory:
rm -rf .git/modules/libs/shared-lib

git commit -m "Remove shared-lib submodule"

article_steps.title: Subtree vs Submodule
article_steps.content: Git subtree embeds another repository's files directly into your project tree. Unlike submodules, the files are actually committed to your repository. No special clone commands needed — it just works for anyone who clones your repo.

article_steps.title: Add a Subtree
article_steps.content: Pull an external repository into a subdirectory:
article_steps.command: git subtree add --prefix=libs/shared-lib https://github.com/user/shared-lib.git main --squash

article_steps.title: Update from Upstream
article_steps.content: Pull the latest changes from the external repo:
article_steps.command: git subtree pull --prefix=libs/shared-lib https://github.com/user/shared-lib.git main --squash

article_steps.title: Push Changes Upstream
article_steps.content: If you modify the subtree files, you can push changes back:
article_steps.command: git subtree push --prefix=libs/shared-lib https://github.com/user/shared-lib.git main

article_steps.title: Subtree Pros and Cons
article_steps.content:
Pros:
- No special setup for cloners
- Files are directly in the repo
- Works with standard Git commands
- No .gitmodules file to manage

Cons:
- Repository size grows (includes all subtree files)
- History can become cluttered
- Updates from upstream require explicit pulls

article_steps.title: What is an Upstream Branch?
article_steps.content: An upstream (tracking) branch is the remote branch that your local branch is linked to. When configured, you can simply type 'git push' or 'git pull' without specifying origin and branch name each time.

article_steps.title: Set Upstream When Pushing
article_steps.content: The most common way to set upstream is with your first push:
article_steps.command:
git push -u origin feature-branch
# -u is short for --set-upstream
# After this, 'git push' and 'git pull' work without arguments

article_steps.title: Set Upstream Explicitly
article_steps.content: Link a local branch to a remote branch:
article_steps.command:
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main
# Or the shorter form:
git branch -u origin/main

article_steps.title: Check Upstream Configuration
article_steps.content: See the upstream configuration for all branches:
article_steps.command:
git branch -vv
# Shows [origin/main] next to branches that have upstream set

article_steps.title: Configure Auto-Setup
article_steps.content: Make Git automatically set up tracking for new branches:
article_steps.command:
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true
# Now 'git push' on a new branch automatically sets upstream

article_steps.title: The Problem with --force
article_steps.content: git push --force overwrites the remote branch unconditionally. If a teammate pushed commits after your last fetch, their work is lost. This is one of the most dangerous Git operations.

article_steps.title: What --force-with-lease Does
article_steps.content: Force-with-lease only force pushes if the remote branch is exactly where you think it is. If someone else has pushed new commits since your last fetch, the push is rejected, protecting their work.
article_steps.command: git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch

article_steps.title: When You Need to Force Push
article_steps.content:
Force pushing is necessary after:
- Rebasing a branch (commits have new hashes)
- Amending a pushed commit
- Squashing commits that were already pushed
- Using interactive rebase on a pushed branch

article_steps.title: Always Use --force-with-lease
article_steps.content: Make force-with-lease your default by creating an alias:
article_steps.command:
git config --global alias.fpush "push --force-with-lease"
# Now use:
git fpush origin feature-branch

article_steps.title: WARNING: Know the Limitations
article_steps.content:
Force-with-lease checks against your local remote-tracking ref. If you run 'git fetch' before force pushing, your local ref updates and force-with-lease won't protect against the new commits. Always verify before force pushing:

1. Communicate with your team
2. Check the remote branch log
3. Only force push to branches you own

article_steps.title: The Problem
article_steps.content: When remote branches are deleted (after merging PRs), your local Git still keeps references to them. Over time, 'git branch -r' shows many stale branches that no longer exist on the server.

article_steps.title: See Stale Branches
article_steps.content: List remote branches that no longer exist:
article_steps.command:
git remote prune origin --dry-run
# Shows what would be pruned without actually doing it

article_steps.title: Prune Stale References
article_steps.content: Remove references to deleted remote branches:
article_steps.command:
git fetch --prune
# Or specifically:
git remote prune origin

article_steps.title: Auto-Prune on Fetch
article_steps.content: Configure Git to prune automatically every time you fetch:
article_steps.command:
git config --global fetch.prune true
# Now 'git fetch' always cleans up stale references

article_steps.title: Clean Up Local Branches Too
article_steps.content: Delete local branches whose remote counterpart is gone:
article_steps.command:
# List merged branches (safe to delete):
git branch --merged main

# Delete them:
git branch --merged main | grep -v main | xargs git branch -d

article_steps.title: Why Fetch Selectively?
article_steps.content: In large repositories with many branches, fetching everything can be slow and waste bandwidth. You might only need one or two branches for your current work.

article_steps.title: Fetch a Specific Branch
article_steps.content: Download just one branch from the remote:
article_steps.command:
git fetch origin feature-branch
# Only fetches the specified branch

article_steps.title: Clone a Single Branch
article_steps.content: Clone only one branch from the start:
article_steps.command:
git clone --single-branch --branch main https://github.com/user/repo.git
# Only main is downloaded

article_steps.title: Fetch a Branch That Was Not Cloned
article_steps.content: If you used --single-branch and need another branch later:
article_steps.command:
# Add the branch to your fetch configuration:
git remote set-branches --add origin other-branch
git fetch origin other-branch
git switch other-branch

article_steps.title: Use Refspecs for Advanced Control
article_steps.content: Refspecs define exactly what to fetch:
article_steps.command:
# Fetch a specific remote branch to a local name:
git fetch origin feature-branch:my-local-name

# Fetch all branches matching a pattern:
git fetch origin 'refs/heads/release/*:refs/remotes/origin/release/*'

article_steps.title: File Deleted but Not Committed
article_steps.content: If you deleted a file but have not committed yet, restore it from the index:
article_steps.command:
git restore filename.txt
# or older syntax:
git checkout -- filename.txt

article_steps.title: File Deleted and Committed
article_steps.content: If the deletion was committed, restore from the commit before the deletion:
article_steps.command:
# Find when the file was deleted:
git log --diff-filter=D --summary -- path/to/file.txt

# Restore from the commit just before deletion:
git checkout abc1234^ -- path/to/file.txt
# The ^ means 'parent of that commit'

article_steps.title: Find a Deleted File by Name
article_steps.content: If you don't remember the exact path:
article_steps.command:
# Search for the file name in history:
git log --all --full-history -- "**/filename.txt"

# Or search for any file matching a pattern:
git log --diff-filter=D --name-only --pretty=format: | grep "pattern"

article_steps.title: Restore and Commit
article_steps.content: After restoring, commit the recovered file:
article_steps.command:
git add restored-file.txt
git commit -m "Restore accidentally deleted file"

article_steps.title: What is Git Bisect?
article_steps.content: Git bisect uses binary search to find which commit introduced a bug. Instead of checking every commit one by one, it repeatedly halves the range of suspect commits. For 1000 commits, bisect needs only about 10 steps.

article_steps.title: Start Bisecting
article_steps.content: Begin the bisect session:
article_steps.command:
git bisect start

# Mark the current commit as bad (has the bug):
git bisect bad

# Mark a known good commit (before the bug existed):
git bisect good abc1234

article_steps.title: Test and Mark Each Checkpoint
article_steps.content: Git checks out a commit in the middle. Test your code, then tell Git the result:
article_steps.command:
# If this commit has the bug:
git bisect bad

# If this commit does NOT have the bug:
git bisect good

# Git automatically checks out the next commit to test

article_steps.title: Find the Guilty Commit
article_steps.content:
After several steps, Git identifies the exact commit:

abc1234 is the first bad commit
commit abc1234
Author: John Doe
Date: Mon Aug 1

    Add payment processing module

article_steps.title: End the Bisect Session
article_steps.content: Return to your original branch:
article_steps.command:
git bisect reset
# Returns you to the branch you were on before bisecting

article_steps.title: Automate with a Script
article_steps.content: If you have a test script, automate the entire process:
article_steps.command:
git bisect start HEAD abc1234
git bisect run npm test
# Git automatically runs the test at each step and marks good/bad

article_steps.title: Why Not Just Reset?
article_steps.content: If a commit has been pushed to a shared branch, using 'git reset' and force pushing would rewrite history and break things for everyone who has pulled those commits. The safe approach is 'git revert'.

article_steps.title: Revert the Last Pushed Commit
article_steps.content: Create a new commit that undoes the changes:
article_steps.command:
git revert HEAD
# This creates a new commit that reverses the changes
# Then push the revert:
git push origin main

article_steps.title: Revert a Specific Commit
article_steps.content: Undo any commit, not just the last one:
article_steps.command:
git revert abc1234
git push origin main

article_steps.title: Revert Without Auto-Committing
article_steps.content: If you want to review or modify the revert before committing:
article_steps.command:
git revert --no-commit abc1234
# Changes are staged but not committed
# Review, modify if needed, then:
git commit -m "Revert: remove broken payment feature"

article_steps.title: Verify the Revert
article_steps.content: Confirm the revert worked correctly:
article_steps.command:
# See the revert commit:
git log --oneline -3

# Verify the code is back to the expected state:
git diff HEAD~2..HEAD
# Should show the inverse of the original commit's changes

article_steps.title: Revert a Range of Commits
article_steps.content: Revert multiple consecutive commits in one go:
article_steps.command:
# Revert commits from abc1234 to def5678 (exclusive..inclusive):
git revert abc1234..def5678

# This creates one revert commit per original commit

article_steps.title: Revert Into a Single Commit
article_steps.content: Combine multiple reverts into one clean commit:
article_steps.command:
git revert --no-commit abc1234..def5678
# All reverts are staged but not committed
git commit -m "Revert: remove feature X (commits abc1234 to def5678)"

article_steps.title: Revert Specific Non-Consecutive Commits
article_steps.content: Cherry-pick which commits to revert:
article_steps.command:
git revert --no-commit abc1234
git revert --no-commit ghi9012
git revert --no-commit mno3456
git commit -m "Revert three specific commits"

article_steps.title: Handle Conflicts During Multi-Revert
article_steps.content: If conflicts arise while reverting multiple commits:
article_steps.command:
# Fix the conflict, then continue:
git add .
git revert --continue

# Or abort the entire operation:
git revert --abort

article_steps.title: View a File at a Specific Commit
article_steps.content: See what a file looked like at any point in history:
article_steps.command: git show abc1234:path/to/file.js

article_steps.title: Restore a File from a Specific Commit
article_steps.content: Replace the current version with a historical version:
article_steps.command:
# Modern syntax (Git 2.23+):
git restore --source=abc1234 -- path/to/file.js

# Traditional syntax:
git checkout abc1234 -- path/to/file.js

article_steps.title: Restore from a Branch
article_steps.content: Get a file from another branch:
article_steps.command:
git restore --source=feature-branch -- path/to/file.js
# The file is now in your working directory with the other branch's version

article_steps.title: Commit the Restored File
article_steps.content: After restoring, commit the change:
article_steps.command:
git add path/to/file.js
git commit -m "Restore file.js from commit abc1234"

article_steps.title: What Does Git Clean Do?
article_steps.content: Git clean removes files that are not tracked by Git — files that have never been added or committed. This is useful for removing build artifacts, temporary files, or generated code that is cluttering your working directory.

article_steps.title: Preview What Would Be Deleted
article_steps.content: Always do a dry run first:
article_steps.command:
git clean -n
# Shows what WOULD be removed without actually deleting anything

article_steps.title: Remove Untracked Files
article_steps.content: WARNING: This permanently deletes files. They cannot be recovered through Git.
article_steps.command:
# Remove untracked files:
git clean -f

# Remove untracked files AND directories:
git clean -fd

article_steps.title: Remove Ignored Files Too
article_steps.content: Also remove files matched by .gitignore:
article_steps.command:
# Remove only ignored files (like build artifacts):
git clean -fX

# Remove both untracked and ignored files:
git clean -fdx

article_steps.title: Interactive Mode
article_steps.content: Select which files to clean interactively:
article_steps.command:
git clean -i
# Shows a menu to select specific files to remove

article_steps.title: How Rebase Can Go Wrong
article_steps.content:
A rebase can go wrong when:
- You accidentally rebase onto the wrong branch
- Conflicts were resolved incorrectly
- The rebase introduced subtle bugs
- You rebased commits that were already pushed

article_steps.title: Find the Pre-Rebase State
article_steps.content: Use reflog to find where your branch was before the rebase:
article_steps.command:
git reflog
# Look for the entry just before 'rebase (start)':
# abc1234 HEAD@{5}: rebase (start): checkout main
# def5678 HEAD@{6}: commit: Your last commit before rebase  <-- this one

article_steps.title: Reset to Pre-Rebase State
article_steps.content: Move your branch back to where it was:

article_steps.title: If You Already Pushed the Bad Rebase
article_steps.content: If the rebased commits were force-pushed, you need to force push the recovery:
article_steps.command:
# After resetting locally:
git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch
# Warn teammates to re-fetch

article_steps.title: Prevent Future Issues
article_steps.content: Before rebasing, create a backup branch:
article_steps.command:
git branch backup-before-rebase
git rebase main
# If something goes wrong:
git reset --hard backup-before-rebase

article_steps.title: The Problem
article_steps.content: You were working and made a commit, then realized you are on 'main' instead of your feature branch. The commit needs to be moved to the correct branch.

article_steps.title: Method 1: Cherry-Pick and Reset
article_steps.content: Copy the commit to the right branch, then remove it from the wrong one:
article_steps.command:
# Note the commit hash:
git log --oneline -1
# Output: abc1234 Add login feature

# Switch to the correct branch:
git switch feature-branch

# Copy the commit:
git cherry-pick abc1234

# Go back and remove from wrong branch:
git switch main
git reset --hard HEAD~1

article_steps.title: Method 2: Create New Branch (if not pushed)
article_steps.content: If you need a new branch for this commit:
article_steps.command:
# Create a branch from the current state:
git switch -c feature-login

# The new branch has your commit
# Now fix the original branch:
git switch main
git reset --hard HEAD~1

article_steps.title: If Already Pushed to Wrong Branch
article_steps.content: If the commit was pushed to the remote wrong branch, revert it instead of resetting:
article_steps.command:
# Copy to correct branch:
git switch feature-branch
git cherry-pick abc1234
git push origin feature-branch

# Revert on wrong branch:
git switch main
git revert HEAD
git push origin main

article_steps.title: The Situation
article_steps.content: You ran 'git add' to stage files but realized you don't want to include all of them in the next commit. You need to unstage some files without losing your changes.

article_steps.title: Unstage a Specific File
article_steps.content: Remove a file from the staging area (keeps changes in working directory):
article_steps.command:
# Modern syntax (Git 2.23+):
git restore --staged filename.txt

# Traditional syntax:
git reset HEAD filename.txt

article_steps.title: Unstage All Files
article_steps.content: Remove everything from staging:
article_steps.command:
# Modern syntax:
git restore --staged .

# Traditional syntax:
git reset HEAD

article_steps.title: Verify the Unstaging
article_steps.content: Check that files are back to 'modified but unstaged':
article_steps.command:
git status
# Files should now appear under 'Changes not staged for commit'

article_steps.title: Important: Your Changes are Safe
article_steps.content: Unstaging does NOT delete your changes. It only moves files from the 'staged' area back to the 'modified' state. Your actual file contents remain exactly as they are.

article_steps.title: When git commit --amend Is Not Enough
article_steps.content: The --amend flag only works on the most recent commit. To edit older commits, you need interactive rebase.

article_steps.title: Start Interactive Rebase
article_steps.content: Go back to the commit you want to edit:
article_steps.command:
# To edit a commit 5 commits ago:
git rebase -i HEAD~5

article_steps.title: Mark the Commit for Editing
article_steps.content:
In the editor, change 'pick' to 'edit' for the commit you want to modify:

pick abc1234 Add authentication
edit def5678 Add payment module    ← change this line
pick ghi9012 Update README

article_steps.title: Make Your Changes
article_steps.content: Git pauses at the marked commit. Make your changes:
article_steps.command:
# Edit files as needed...

# Stage the changes:
git add .

# Amend the commit:
git commit --amend -m "Add payment module with validation"

# Continue the rebase:
git rebase --continue

article_steps.title: Using Fixup (Automated Approach)
article_steps.content: If you just need to add forgotten changes to an older commit:
article_steps.command:
# Make the fix and commit it:
git add forgotten-file.js
git commit --fixup=def5678

# Then auto-squash:
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5
# The fixup commit is automatically placed and squashed

article_steps.title: What are Worktrees?
article_steps.content: A worktree is a linked working directory attached to your repository. Each worktree checks out a different branch, letting you work on multiple branches simultaneously in separate folders without switching branches or stashing changes.

article_steps.title: Add a Worktree
article_steps.content: Create a new worktree for a different branch:
article_steps.command:
# Create a worktree for the hotfix branch:
git worktree add ../project-hotfix hotfix-branch

# Create a worktree with a new branch:
git worktree add ../project-feature -b new-feature

article_steps.title: Work in Multiple Branches
article_steps.content:
Now you have two directories, each on a different branch:

/project/ → main branch (your primary worktree)
/project-hotfix/ → hotfix-branch
/project-feature/ → new-feature

Edit files in any directory independently. Commits, pulls, and pushes work normally in each.

article_steps.title: List and Remove Worktrees
article_steps.content: Manage your worktrees:
article_steps.command:
# List all worktrees:
git worktree list

# Remove a worktree when done:
git worktree remove ../project-hotfix

# Force remove (if there are changes):
git worktree remove --force ../project-hotfix

article_steps.title: Use Cases
article_steps.content:
Worktrees are great for:
- Working on a hotfix while a feature is in progress
- Running tests on one branch while coding on another
- Reviewing a PR locally without disrupting your work
- Comparing behavior between two branches side by side

article_steps.title: Why Merge Reverts Are Special
article_steps.content: A regular commit has one parent. A merge commit has two parents. When reverting, Git needs to know which parent to revert to — the mainline or the merged branch. You must specify this with the -m flag.

article_steps.title: Revert a Merge Commit
article_steps.content: Use -m 1 to keep the mainline (usually main branch) and undo the merged changes:
article_steps.command:
git revert -m 1 abc1234
# -m 1 means 'keep parent 1 (main branch)'
# -m 2 would keep parent 2 (the merged branch)

article_steps.title: Understanding -m 1 vs -m 2
article_steps.content:
For a merge commit created by 'git merge feature into main':

-m 1: Undo the feature changes, keep main as it was
-m 2: Undo the main changes, keep feature as it was

You almost always want -m 1.

article_steps.title: The Re-Merge Problem
article_steps.content: WARNING: After reverting a merge, you cannot simply re-merge the same branch later. Git thinks those changes are already integrated. To re-merge, you must first revert the revert:
article_steps.command:
# Step 1: Revert the merge
git revert -m 1 abc1234

# Step 2: Later, to re-merge the branch,
# first revert the revert:
git revert def5678  # hash of the revert commit

# Step 3: Now merge the branch again:
git merge feature-branch

article_steps.title: Verify the Revert
article_steps.content: Confirm the merge revert worked:
article_steps.command:
git log --oneline -5
# Should show the revert commit

git diff HEAD~1
# Should show the inverse of the merged changes

article_steps.title: What Causes This Error
article_steps.content:
This error occurs when two branches have completely independent histories with no common ancestor commit. Common scenarios:

1. You created a new repo on GitHub with a README, then tried to push a local repo
2. You are merging two separate repositories
3. You are pulling from a different project entirely

article_steps.title: The Fix
article_steps.content: Allow Git to merge the unrelated histories:
article_steps.command:
# For pull:
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories

# For merge:
git merge other-branch --allow-unrelated-histories

article_steps.title: Resolve Any Conflicts
article_steps.content: After allowing unrelated histories, you may have conflicts (especially in README.md or other common files). Resolve them normally:
article_steps.command:
# Check for conflicts:
git status

# Fix conflicts, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Merge unrelated histories"

article_steps.title: Prevention
article_steps.content:
To avoid this in the future:
- When creating a GitHub repo, do NOT initialize with README if you already have a local repo
- Clone the empty repo first, then add your files
- Or create the repo without any files, then push your local code

article_steps.title: Why This Happens
article_steps.content: Git refuses to switch branches or pull when you have uncommitted changes that would conflict with files in the target branch. Git is protecting your work from being lost.

article_steps.title: Option 1: Stash Your Changes
article_steps.content: Temporarily save your changes, perform the operation, then restore:
article_steps.command:
git stash
git switch other-branch
# Do your work on the other branch
git switch original-branch
git stash pop

article_steps.title: Option 2: Commit Your Changes
article_steps.content: If your changes are ready, commit them first:
article_steps.command:
git add .
git commit -m "Work in progress: save current state"
git switch other-branch

article_steps.title: Option 3: Discard Your Changes
article_steps.content: WARNING: This permanently loses your uncommitted work:
article_steps.command:
# Discard changes in specific files:
git restore file1.js file2.js

# Discard ALL uncommitted changes:
git restore .
git clean -fd

article_steps.title: Option 4: Force Checkout (Dangerous)
article_steps.content: Force switch branches and discard conflicting changes:
article_steps.command:
git checkout -f other-branch
# WARNING: Permanently discards conflicting uncommitted changes

article_steps.title: What Triggers This Warning
article_steps.content:
You enter detached HEAD state when you check out:
- A specific commit hash: git checkout abc1234
- A tag: git checkout v1.0.0
- A remote branch directly: git checkout origin/main

In this state, HEAD points to a commit, not a branch.

article_steps.title: Is It Dangerous?
article_steps.content: Not immediately. You can look around, run tests, and even make commits. The risk is that commits made in detached HEAD are not on any branch and can be lost when you switch away.

article_steps.title: Return to a Branch
article_steps.content: Simply switch to an existing branch:
article_steps.command:
git switch main
# or:
git checkout main

article_steps.title: Save Your Detached HEAD Work
article_steps.content: If you made valuable commits in detached HEAD, save them:
article_steps.command:
# Create a new branch at the current position:
git switch -c rescue-branch
# All your commits are now safely on this branch

article_steps.title: Checkout a Tag Without Detaching
article_steps.content: If you want to work on a tag, create a branch from it:
article_steps.command:
# Instead of:
git checkout v1.0.0

# Do this:
git switch -c fix-v1.0.0 v1.0.0
# Now you're on a branch based on the tag

article_steps.title: What is Git LFS?
article_steps.content: Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces large files (images, videos, datasets) with lightweight pointers in your repository. The actual file contents are stored on a separate LFS server, keeping your repo fast.

article_steps.title: Install and Configure LFS
article_steps.content: Set up Git LFS in your repository:
article_steps.command:
# Install LFS:
git lfs install

# Track specific file types:
git lfs track "*.psd"
git lfs track "*.mp4"
git lfs track "*.zip"

# Make sure .gitattributes is tracked:
git add .gitattributes

article_steps.title: Common Issue: Files Not Being Tracked
article_steps.content: If LFS is not tracking files as expected:
article_steps.command:
# Check which files are tracked by LFS:
git lfs ls-files

# Check tracking rules:
cat .gitattributes

# If a file was committed before LFS was set up, migrate it:
git lfs migrate import --include="*.psd"

article_steps.title: Common Issue: Smudge/Clean Errors
article_steps.content: If you see 'smudge filter lfs failed':
article_steps.command:
# Re-install LFS hooks:
git lfs install --force

# Pull LFS objects:
git lfs pull

# If still failing, check your LFS server:
git lfs env

article_steps.title: Bandwidth and Storage Limits
article_steps.content:
GitHub Free includes 1 GB LFS storage and 1 GB/month bandwidth.

If you hit limits:
- Purchase additional LFS data packs
- Move large files to external storage (S3, CDN)
- Use .gitattributes carefully to track only necessary files

Check usage:
article_steps.command:
git lfs env
# Shows your LFS endpoint and configuration

article_steps.title: Common Causes of Slow Git
article_steps.content:
Git can slow down due to:
- Very large number of files (100,000+)
- Large file sizes in history
- Too many pack files
- Unoptimized configuration
- Network issues with remote operations

article_steps.title: Run Garbage Collection
article_steps.content: Clean up and optimize your repository:
article_steps.command:
# Basic garbage collection:
git gc

# Aggressive optimization (takes longer):
git gc --aggressive --prune=now

article_steps.title: Enable Background Maintenance
article_steps.content: Let Git optimize itself automatically:
article_steps.command:
git maintenance start
# Sets up automatic background tasks:
# - Prefetch: fetch remotes hourly
# - Commit-graph: optimize commit lookups
# - Pack-refs: compress references
# - Loose-objects: clean up loose objects

article_steps.title: Optimize for Large Repos
article_steps.content: Configure Git for better performance with many files:
article_steps.command:
# Enable filesystem monitor (speeds up status/diff):
git config core.fsmonitor true

# Enable untracked cache:
git config core.untrackedCache true

# Use commit graph for faster log operations:
git config fetch.writeCommitGraph true

article_steps.title: Check Repository Size
article_steps.content: Understand what is taking up space:
article_steps.command:
# Check total repo size:
du -sh .git

# Find the largest objects:
git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | sort -k3 -n -r | head -20

article_steps.title: The Problem
article_steps.content: Windows uses CRLF (\r\n) line endings. Mac/Linux use LF (\n). When team members use different operating systems, Git may show entire files as changed even though only line endings differ.

article_steps.title: Configure Git for Your OS
article_steps.content: Set the appropriate autocrlf setting:
article_steps.command:
# On Windows (converts LF to CRLF on checkout, CRLF to LF on commit):
git config --global core.autocrlf true

# On Mac/Linux (converts CRLF to LF on commit, no conversion on checkout):
git config --global core.autocrlf input

article_steps.title: Use .gitattributes (Recommended)
article_steps.content: Create a .gitattributes file for consistent behavior across all developers:
article_steps.command:
# .gitattributes
* text=auto
*.sh text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
*.jpg binary

article_steps.title: Fix Existing Files
article_steps.content: Renormalize all files to apply the new settings:
article_steps.command:
git add --renormalize .
git commit -m "Fix line endings"

article_steps.title: Verify Line Endings
article_steps.content: Check what line endings a file uses:
article_steps.command:
# On Mac/Linux:
file filename.txt
# Shows 'ASCII text' (LF) or 'ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators'

# Check Git's stored endings:
git ls-files --eol

article_steps.title: Signs of Corruption
article_steps.content:
A corrupted repository may show errors like:
- 'fatal: bad object HEAD'
- 'error: object file is empty'
- 'fatal: loose object is corrupt'
- 'error: unable to read sha1 file'

Corruption can be caused by disk failures, power outages, or interrupted Git operations.

article_steps.title: Run File System Check
article_steps.content: Diagnose corruption with git fsck:
article_steps.command:
git fsck --full
# Reports missing objects, dangling commits, and corruption

article_steps.title: Try Simple Fixes First
article_steps.content: Sometimes simple steps resolve the issue:
article_steps.command:
# Rebuild the index:
rm .git/index
git reset

# Fix HEAD reference:
echo 'ref: refs/heads/main' > .git/HEAD

# Fetch from remote to get missing objects:
git fetch origin

article_steps.title: Recover from Remote
article_steps.content: If you have a remote copy, the easiest fix is often:
article_steps.command:
# Back up your current work:
cp -r . ../project-backup

# Re-clone from remote:
cd ..
git clone https://github.com/user/project.git project-recovered

# Copy uncommitted changes from backup:
cp -r project-backup/src/* project-recovered/src/

article_steps.title: Prevention
article_steps.content:
Prevent corruption:

1. Never kill Git processes forcefully
2. Use a UPS or reliable power supply
3. Keep regular remote backups (push frequently)
4. Avoid using Git on network-mounted filesystems
5. Run 'git fsck' periodically as a health check

article_steps.title: What Causes Bad Object Errors
article_steps.content:
These errors occur when Git references an object (commit, tree, blob) that doesn't exist or is corrupted. Common causes:

- Interrupted Git operations (force quit during rebase)
- Disk corruption
- Manual editing of .git directory
- Failed garbage collection

article_steps.title: Diagnose the Problem
article_steps.content: Find which objects are missing or broken:
article_steps.command: git fsck --full --no-dangling 2>&1 | head -20

article_steps.title: Fetch Missing Objects
article_steps.content: If the objects exist on the remote, fetch them:
article_steps.command:
git fetch --all
# This downloads any objects that exist remotely but are missing locally

article_steps.title: Remove Bad References
article_steps.content: If a branch or tag points to a bad object:
article_steps.command:
# For a bad branch reference:
git branch -D bad-branch

# For a bad tag:
git tag -d bad-tag

# Then re-fetch:
git fetch origin

article_steps.title: Last Resort: Re-clone
article_steps.content: If nothing else works, re-clone the repository:
article_steps.command:
# Save any local-only work:
git format-patch origin/main --stdout > my-patches.patch

# Re-clone:
cd ..
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
cd repo

# Re-apply your patches:
git am < ../my-patches.patch

article_steps.title: What Causes This Error
article_steps.content: Git creates a .git/index.lock file when performing operations that modify the index (add, commit, merge). If Git crashes or is interrupted, the lock file may be left behind, blocking all subsequent operations.

article_steps.title: The Error Message
article_steps.content:
You see:
fatal: Unable to create '/path/to/repo/.git/index.lock': File exists.

Another git process seems to be running in this repository.
If no other git process is running, remove the file manually.

article_steps.title: Check for Running Git Processes
article_steps.content: First, make sure no Git operation is actually running:
article_steps.command:
# On Mac/Linux:
ps aux | grep git

# On Windows:
tasklist | findstr git

article_steps.title: Remove the Lock File
article_steps.content: If no Git process is running, safely remove the lock:
article_steps.command:
# On Mac/Linux:
rm -f .git/index.lock

# On Windows:
del .git\index.lock

# Or force delete on Windows:
rm -Force .git/index.lock

article_steps.title: Verify Git Works
article_steps.content: After removing the lock, verify Git operations work:
article_steps.command:
git status
# Should work normally now

article_steps.title: Common Hook Issues
article_steps.content:
Git hooks can fail due to:
- Missing execute permissions (Linux/Mac)
- Wrong shebang line (#!/bin/sh vs #!/bin/bash)
- Missing dependencies (Node.js, Python not installed)
- Path issues (hook can't find tools)
- Windows line ending issues in hook scripts

article_steps.title: Check Permissions
article_steps.content: Ensure hook files are executable:
article_steps.command:
# Check permissions:
ls -la .git/hooks/pre-commit

# Make executable:
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

article_steps.title: Debug a Failing Hook
article_steps.content: Add debugging output to your hook:
article_steps.command:
# Add to the top of your hook script:
set -x  # Enable command tracing
echo "Hook running from: $(pwd)"
echo "PATH: $PATH"
echo "Node: $(which node)"

article_steps.title: Skip Hooks Temporarily
article_steps.content: Bypass hooks when needed:
article_steps.command:
# Skip pre-commit and commit-msg hooks:
git commit --no-verify -m "Emergency fix"

# Skip pre-push hooks:
git push --no-verify

article_steps.title: Fix Husky Hook Issues
article_steps.content: If using Husky for team hooks:
article_steps.command:
# Reinstall Husky:
npx husky install

# Ensure .husky directory exists:
ls -la .husky/

# Check if the hook is valid:
cat .husky/pre-commit

article_steps.title: What Causes This Error
article_steps.content:
This error means Git cannot find the branch you are trying to push. The most common causes:

1. No commits exist yet (empty repository)
2. The branch name is different (master vs main)
3. Typo in the branch name

article_steps.title: Cause 1: No Commits
article_steps.content: You cannot push an empty repository. Make at least one commit first:
article_steps.command:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push -u origin main

article_steps.title: Cause 2: Wrong Branch Name
article_steps.content: Check your actual branch name:
article_steps.command:
git branch
# If it shows 'master' but you're pushing 'main':
git push -u origin master

# Or rename your branch:
git branch -m master main
git push -u origin main

article_steps.title: Cause 3: Typo
article_steps.content: Double-check the branch name:
article_steps.command:
# See all local branches:
git branch

# See all remote branches:
git branch -r

# Push with the correct name:
git push origin correct-branch-name

article_steps.title: Enable Verbose Output
article_steps.content: Get detailed information about network operations:
article_steps.command:
# For HTTPS operations:
GIT_CURL_VERBOSE=1 git fetch origin

# For SSH operations:
GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -v' git fetch origin

article_steps.title: Fix SSL Certificate Errors
article_steps.content: If you see SSL certificate verification errors:
article_steps.command:
# Update CA certificates (recommended):
# Mac: brew install ca-certificates
# Ubuntu: sudo apt update && sudo apt install ca-certificates

# Last resort: disable SSL verification (NOT recommended for production):
git config --global http.sslVerify false

article_steps.title: Configure Proxy Settings
article_steps.content: If you are behind a corporate proxy:
article_steps.command:
# Set HTTP proxy:
git config --global http.proxy http://proxy.company.com:8080

# Set HTTPS proxy:
git config --global https.proxy http://proxy.company.com:8080

# Remove proxy settings:
git config --global --unset http.proxy

article_steps.title: Fix Timeout Issues
article_steps.content: Increase timeout for slow connections:
article_steps.command:
# Increase HTTP timeout (default is no timeout):
git config --global http.lowSpeedLimit 1000
git config --global http.lowSpeedTime 60

# Increase buffer size for large repos:
git config --global http.postBuffer 524288000

article_steps.title: Switch Between HTTPS and SSH
article_steps.content: If one protocol fails, try the other:
article_steps.command:
# Switch from HTTPS to SSH:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git

# Switch from SSH to HTTPS:
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Common HTTPS Errors
article_steps.content:
You may see errors like:
- fatal: unable to access 'https://...': Could not resolve host
- fatal: unable to access 'https://...': Failed to connect
- The requested URL returned error: 403
- The requested URL returned error: 401

article_steps.title: Check Your Remote URL
article_steps.content: Verify the remote URL is correct:
article_steps.command:
git remote -v
# Make sure the URL matches your actual repository

article_steps.title: Fix 401/403 Authentication Errors
article_steps.content: These mean your credentials are wrong or expired:
article_steps.command:
# Update your credentials:
git config --global credential.helper manager-core

# Or use a new Personal Access Token:
git remote set-url origin https://YOUR_TOKEN@github.com/user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Fix DNS Resolution Errors
article_steps.content: If Git cannot resolve the hostname:
article_steps.command:
# Test DNS resolution:
nslookup github.com
# or:
ping github.com

# If DNS fails, try:
# 1. Check your internet connection
# 2. Try a different DNS server (8.8.8.8)
# 3. Check if the site is blocked by firewall

article_steps.title: Fix Connection Refused
article_steps.content: If the connection is refused or times out:
article_steps.command:
# Check if the server is reachable:
curl -I https://github.com

# If behind a proxy, configure it:
git config --global http.proxy http://proxy:port

# If all else fails, try SSH instead:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git

article_steps.title: Common Submodule Errors
article_steps.content:
Frequent submodule issues:
- 'fatal: no submodule mapping found' – .gitmodules is missing or wrong
- Empty submodule directories after cloning
- 'reference is not a tree' – submodule points to a nonexistent commit
- Permission denied when accessing submodule repo

article_steps.title: Fix Empty Submodule Directories
article_steps.content: If submodule directories are empty after cloning:
article_steps.command:
# Initialize and update all submodules:
git submodule init
git submodule update

# Or do both at once:
git submodule update --init --recursive

article_steps.title: Fix URL Mismatch
article_steps.content: If the submodule URL has changed:
article_steps.command:
# Sync URLs from .gitmodules to .git/config:
git submodule sync

# Then update:
git submodule update --init --recursive

article_steps.title: Fix 'reference is not a tree'
article_steps.content: This happens when the parent repo points to a submodule commit that doesn't exist:
article_steps.command:
# Enter the submodule directory:
cd path/to/submodule

# Fetch all commits:
git fetch --all

# If the commit exists, checkout:
git checkout abc1234

# If the commit doesn't exist, update to latest:
git checkout main
cd ..
git add path/to/submodule
git commit -m "Update submodule to latest"

article_steps.title: Force Reinitialize
article_steps.content: Nuclear option — completely reset submodules:
article_steps.command:
# Remove all submodule directories:
git submodule deinit --all -f

# Remove the submodule caches:
rm -rf .git/modules/*

# Re-initialize:
git submodule init
git submodule update --recursive

article_steps.title: Mistake 1: Adding .gitignore After Tracking
article_steps.content: The most common mistake. If a file is already tracked by Git, adding it to .gitignore will NOT stop tracking it.
article_steps.command:
# Fix: Remove the file from tracking (keeps it locally):
git rm --cached filename.txt
git commit -m "Stop tracking filename.txt"

# For a directory:
git rm -r --cached node_modules/
git commit -m "Stop tracking node_modules"

article_steps.title: Mistake 2: Wrong Pattern Syntax
article_steps.content:
Common pattern errors:

# Wrong (matches nothing):
/node_modules

# Correct (matches the directory anywhere):
node_modules/

# Wrong (too specific):
src/components/*.test.js

# Correct (matches recursively):
**/*.test.js

article_steps.title: Mistake 3: Negation Not Working
article_steps.content: Negation patterns (!) don't work if a parent directory is ignored:
article_steps.command:
# This DOES NOT work:
build/
!build/important.js

# Because the build/ directory itself is ignored
# Fix: Don't ignore the directory, ignore its contents:
build/*
!build/important.js

article_steps.title: Debug .gitignore Rules
article_steps.content: Find out why a file is or is not being ignored:
article_steps.command:
# Check if a file is ignored and which rule applies:
git check-ignore -v filename.txt

# Check multiple files:
git check-ignore -v path/to/file1 path/to/file2

article_steps.title: Global .gitignore
article_steps.content: Ignore files across ALL your repositories:
article_steps.command:
# Create a global gitignore:
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global

# Add common patterns to ~/.gitignore_global:
# .DS_Store
# Thumbs.db
# *.swp
# .idea/
# .vscode/

article_steps.title: What is Git?
article_steps.content: Git is a free, open-source distributed version control system. It helps developers track changes in their code, collaborate with others, and maintain a history of their project. Unlike centralized systems, every developer has a full copy of the repository on their local machine.

article_steps.title: Install Git
article_steps.content: Download Git from the official website at git-scm.com. For Windows, run the installer and follow the default settings. For Mac, you can use Homebrew with the command below. For Linux, use your package manager.
article_steps.command:
# Windows: Download from git-scm.com
# Mac:
brew install git
# Linux (Ubuntu/Debian):
sudo apt-get install git

article_steps.title: Configure Your Identity
article_steps.content: After installing Git, set your name and email. This information is attached to every commit you make.
article_steps.command:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

article_steps.title: Initialize a Repository
article_steps.content: Navigate to your project folder and run the init command to create a new Git repository. This creates a hidden .git folder that tracks all your changes.
article_steps.command:
cd my-project
git init

article_steps.title: Verify Your Setup
article_steps.content: Check that Git is installed and configured correctly by running these commands:
article_steps.command:
git --version
git config --list
