article_faqs.question: Do I need a GitHub account to use Git?
article_faqs.answer: No. Git works locally on your computer. GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting Git repositories. You only need a GitHub account if you want to share your code online.

article_faqs.question: What is the .git folder?
article_faqs.answer: The .git folder is a hidden directory created when you run 'git init'. It contains all the metadata and history for your repository. Do not delete this folder.

article_faqs.question: Can I abort a merge?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. If you want to cancel the merge and go back to the state before, use: git merge --abort

article_faqs.question: How can I prevent merge conflicts?
article_faqs.answer: Pull the latest changes frequently, keep branches short-lived, and communicate with your team about which files you're editing.

article_faqs.question: When is it safe to use force push?
article_faqs.answer: Only use force push when you are working alone on a branch and you are sure nobody else has based work on the remote version of that branch.

article_faqs.question: What scopes should I select for my PAT?
article_faqs.answer: For basic repository access, select the 'repo' scope. If you need to manage workflows, also select 'workflow'.

article_faqs.question: Can I use the same SSH key for multiple GitHub accounts?
article_faqs.answer: You can, but it requires additional configuration in your SSH config file. It's easier to use a separate key for each account.

article_faqs.question: What is a good branch naming convention?
article_faqs.answer: Use descriptive names with prefixes like feature/, bugfix/, or hotfix/. For example: feature/user-login, bugfix/header-alignment.

article_faqs.question: Can I undo a git reset --hard?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, if you act quickly. Use 'git reflog' to find the commit hash before the reset, then use 'git reset --hard <hash>' to recover.

article_faqs.question: What does HEAD~1 mean?
article_faqs.answer: HEAD refers to the current commit. HEAD~1 means 'one commit before HEAD'. HEAD~2 would mean two commits back, and so on.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between clone and fork?
article_faqs.answer: Clone copies a repository to your local machine. Fork copies a repository to your own GitHub account. You typically fork first, then clone your fork.

article_faqs.question: Why not commit directly without staging?
article_faqs.answer: The staging area gives you control over exactly what goes into each commit. You can stage some changes while keeping others for a separate commit.

article_faqs.question: Can I change a commit message after committing?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, for the most recent commit use: git commit --amend -m "New message". For older commits, you would need to use interactive rebase.

article_faqs.question: How long does the reflog keep entries?
article_faqs.answer: By default, reflog entries expire after 90 days. You can change this with: git config gc.reflogExpire 120.days

article_faqs.question: What happens if stash pop causes a conflict?
article_faqs.answer: Git will attempt to apply the stash. If there are conflicts, it will mark them just like merge conflicts. The stash will NOT be dropped in this case — resolve the conflicts, then drop the stash manually with 'git stash drop'.

article_faqs.question: What is 'upstream'?
article_faqs.answer: Upstream typically refers to the original repository that you forked from. You add it as a remote to pull in updates from the original project.

article_faqs.question: Should I use Ed25519 or RSA?
article_faqs.answer: Ed25519 is recommended because it's faster and more secure. RSA is still widely supported if you need compatibility with older systems.

article_faqs.question: Which should I use: fetch or pull?
article_faqs.answer: Use fetch when you want to review changes before merging. Use pull when you trust the changes and want to update quickly. In a team, fetch is often safer.

article_faqs.question: What does 'upstream' mean in git push -u?
article_faqs.answer: The -u flag sets the tracking relationship between your local branch and the remote branch. After setting it once, you can just type 'git push' without specifying the remote and branch.

article_faqs.question: Will I lose my commits in detached HEAD?
article_faqs.answer: Commits made in detached HEAD state are not lost immediately, but they are not on any branch. If you don't create a branch to save them, they may be garbage collected after ~30 days. Use 'git reflog' to find them.

article_faqs.question: Can I recover a deleted branch?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, if you know the last commit hash. Use 'git reflog' to find it, then create a new branch at that commit: git branch recovered-branch abc1234

article_faqs.question: Should I use merge or rebase?
article_faqs.answer: Merge preserves the branch history and is safer for shared branches. Rebase creates a linear history and is cleaner. For beginners, merge is recommended.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between a fork and a clone?
article_faqs.answer: A fork creates a copy on GitHub (server-side). A clone creates a copy on your computer (local). You typically fork first, then clone your fork.

article_faqs.question: How do I sync my fork with the original repo?
article_faqs.answer: Fetch and merge from the upstream remote: git fetch upstream, then git merge upstream/main.

article_faqs.question: Should I choose public or private?
article_faqs.answer: Choose public if you want anyone to see your code (open source, portfolios). Choose private for personal or work projects that should not be visible.

article_faqs.question: Where can I find .gitignore templates?
article_faqs.answer: GitHub provides templates at github.com/github/gitignore for many languages and frameworks (Node.js, Python, Java, etc.).

article_faqs.question: When should I use cherry-pick?
article_faqs.answer: Use cherry-pick when you need a specific fix from another branch but don't want to merge the entire branch. Common for applying hotfixes or moving specific features.

article_faqs.question: How do I exit the git log view?
article_faqs.answer: Press 'q' to quit the log viewer. Git log uses the 'less' pager by default.

article_faqs.question: How do I read diff output?
article_faqs.answer: Lines starting with '-' (red) are removed lines. Lines starting with '+' (green) are added lines. The @@ markers show the line numbers where changes occur.

article_faqs.question: Can I get a summary instead of full diff?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, use 'git diff --stat' to see a summary of how many files changed and how many lines were added/removed in each file.

article_faqs.question: What does 'nothing to commit, working tree clean' mean?
article_faqs.answer: It means all your changes have been committed. There are no modified, staged, or untracked files in your working directory.

article_faqs.question: How do I remove a config setting?
article_faqs.answer: Use 'git config --global --unset setting.name' to remove a specific setting. For example: git config --global --unset core.editor

article_faqs.question: Where is the global config file stored?
article_faqs.answer: On Mac/Linux it's at ~/.gitconfig. On Windows it's at C:\Users\YourName\.gitconfig. You can also edit it directly with 'git config --global --edit'.

article_faqs.question: Is HEAD always on the latest commit?
article_faqs.answer: HEAD points to whatever commit you have checked out. Usually that is the latest commit on your current branch, but you can move HEAD to any commit using checkout or reset.

article_faqs.question: Can I delete an alias?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, use 'git config --global --unset alias.name'. For example: git config --global --unset alias.co

article_faqs.question: What is semantic versioning?
article_faqs.answer: Semantic versioning uses the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., v2.1.3). MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for bug fixes.

article_faqs.question: Can I tag an older commit?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, specify the commit hash: git tag -a v0.9.0 -m "Beta release" abc1234

article_faqs.question: Is there a way to ignore specific commits in blame?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, use 'git blame --ignore-rev <commit-hash>' to skip a specific commit (useful for large formatting changes). You can also create a .git-blame-ignore-revs file.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between git show and git log?
article_faqs.answer: Git log shows a list of commits. Git show displays the full details (including diff) of a single commit. Use log to find commits, then show to inspect one.

article_faqs.question: What if a hunk is too large?
article_faqs.answer: Press 's' to split the hunk into smaller pieces. If it still cannot be split further, press 'e' to manually edit the hunk and choose exactly which lines to stage.

article_faqs.question: Can I switch workflows later?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, workflows are conventions, not Git features. You can evolve your workflow as your team grows. Many teams start with Feature Branch and move to Gitflow or Trunk-Based as needed.

article_faqs.question: Can I run git init in a folder that already has files?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Git init will create the .git directory and start tracking. Your existing files will appear as untracked until you add and commit them.

article_faqs.question: Can I skip a hook temporarily?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, use the --no-verify flag: git commit --no-verify -m "Emergency fix". This skips pre-commit and commit-msg hooks. Use sparingly.

article_faqs.question: Do hooks run on the server?
article_faqs.answer: Server-side hooks (pre-receive, post-receive) run on the Git server. Client-side hooks run on developer machines. GitHub/GitLab provide their own CI/CD instead of server-side hooks.

article_faqs.question: What happens if I rebase after pushing?
article_faqs.answer: Your local and remote histories will diverge. You would need to force push (git push --force-with-lease), which can cause problems for teammates. Always coordinate with your team before force pushing.

article_faqs.question: Should I squash before merging a pull request?
article_faqs.answer: Many teams prefer squashing feature branch commits into one clean commit before merging. GitHub and GitLab offer 'Squash and merge' buttons that do this automatically.

article_faqs.question: Can admins bypass protection rules?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, there is an option to 'Include administrators' in the protection settings. If unchecked, admins can push directly or force push. For maximum safety, include admins.

article_faqs.question: Is Gitflow still recommended?
article_faqs.answer: Gitflow is excellent for projects with scheduled releases. However, for continuous deployment, many teams prefer simpler workflows like GitHub Flow or Trunk-Based Development. Choose based on your release cadence.

article_faqs.question: Will renaming a branch lose my commits?
article_faqs.answer: No. Renaming a branch only changes the label. All commits, history, and file changes are preserved exactly as they were.

article_faqs.question: What happens if the remote branch is deleted?
article_faqs.answer: Your local branch keeps working but loses its tracking reference. Run 'git fetch --prune' to clean up references to deleted remote branches, then set a new upstream if needed.

article_faqs.question: How many long-lived branches should I have?
article_faqs.answer: As few as possible. Most projects need only main. Larger teams may add develop and staging. Each additional branch increases maintenance overhead.

article_faqs.question: What does the '..' notation mean?
article_faqs.answer: The double-dot notation (main..feature) means 'show changes that are in feature but not in main'. Triple-dot (main...feature) shows changes on both sides since the branches diverged.

article_faqs.question: How long should a feature branch live?
article_faqs.answer: Ideally, a few days to two weeks maximum. Long-lived feature branches increase the risk of merge conflicts. Break large features into smaller, mergeable pieces.

article_faqs.question: Should every release have its own branch?
article_faqs.answer: If your team deploys continuously, you may not need release branches. They are most useful when releases are batched and need a stabilization period.

article_faqs.question: Does GitHub's 'Rebase and merge' button rewrite history?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, it rebases your PR commits onto the target branch with new commit hashes. The original commits on your feature branch are unaffected, but the commits on main will have different hashes.

article_faqs.question: Why is it called 'three-way' and not 'two-way'?
article_faqs.answer: A two-way merge would only compare the two branch tips, making it impossible to know which side introduced a change. The third point (common ancestor) tells Git what the original state was, so it can determine what each branch modified.

article_faqs.question: Why is it called 'octopus'?
article_faqs.answer: Like an octopus with many arms, this merge strategy can handle multiple branches at once. The Linux kernel project occasionally uses octopus merges to integrate many subsystem branches.

article_faqs.question: What is the 'ort' strategy?
article_faqs.answer: ORT (Ostensibly Recursive's Twin) is the new default merge strategy since Git 2.34. It replaces 'recursive' with better performance and correctness. It handles the same cases but is significantly faster for large repositories.

article_faqs.question: Can I prevent binary file conflicts?
article_faqs.answer: Minimize binary files in your repository. Use Git LFS (Large File Storage) for large binaries. Coordinate with your team so two people don't modify the same binary file simultaneously.

article_faqs.question: Do I need to install a merge tool separately?
article_faqs.answer: VS Code works if you already have it installed. Other tools like Meld need to be downloaded and installed separately. Git does not include any visual merge tool by default.

article_faqs.question: Can the wrong strategy cause data loss?
article_faqs.answer: No. If a merge strategy cannot resolve conflicts, it will stop and ask you to resolve them manually. No strategy will silently discard your changes (except -s ours, which is intentional).

article_faqs.question: Can I abort and try a different approach?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Use 'git merge --abort' to return to the state before the merge. You can then try rebasing, breaking the merge into smaller steps, or merging intermediate commits.

article_faqs.question: Should I always use --no-ff?
article_faqs.answer: Not always, but --no-ff (no fast-forward) creates a merge commit even when not necessary, making it clear in the history when a branch was integrated. Many teams prefer this for main branch merges.

article_faqs.question: Should I squash or merge?
article_faqs.answer: Squash when the branch has many small, messy commits (WIP, fixup). Merge when the individual commits are meaningful and you want to preserve the detailed history.

article_faqs.question: Can I reopen a closed issue?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, scroll to the bottom of the closed issue and click 'Reopen issue'. All previous comments and history are preserved.

article_faqs.question: Is GitHub Actions free?
article_faqs.answer: GitHub Actions is free for public repositories. Private repositories get 2,000 free minutes per month on the free plan. Additional minutes can be purchased.

article_faqs.question: Can I run Actions locally?
article_faqs.answer: Use the 'act' tool (github.com/nektos/act) to run GitHub Actions locally for testing before pushing.

article_faqs.question: Can I use a static site generator?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. GitHub Pages natively supports Jekyll. You can also use any generator (Hugo, Gatsby, Next.js static export) by building locally and pushing the output, or by using GitHub Actions to build automatically.

article_faqs.question: Can I have multiple PR templates?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Create a PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE directory with multiple .md files. Contributors can choose which template to use by adding ?template=filename.md to the PR URL.

article_faqs.question: Should I use releases for every version?
article_faqs.answer: Create releases for versions that users should know about: major releases, important bug fixes, and security patches. You don't need a release for every internal commit.

article_faqs.question: Is GitHub CLI the same as git?
article_faqs.answer: No. Git manages version control (commits, branches, merges). GitHub CLI (gh) manages GitHub-specific features (PRs, issues, Actions, repos). They complement each other.

article_faqs.question: Are Codespaces free?
article_faqs.answer: GitHub Free users get 120 core-hours per month and 15 GB storage. Pro users get 180 core-hours. Additional usage is billed. Public repos get unlimited codespace hours.

article_faqs.question: How do I stop getting emails from a specific repository?
article_faqs.answer: Go to the repository, click 'Unwatch' at the top, and select 'Participating and @mentions' or 'Ignore'.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between a template and a fork?
article_faqs.answer: Templates create a clean repo with no history and no link to the original. Forks create a copy with full history and maintain a connection to the original repo for pull requests.

article_faqs.question: How long should a code review take?
article_faqs.answer: Reviews should take 30-60 minutes maximum. If a PR is too large to review in that time, ask the author to break it into smaller PRs. Research shows review quality drops significantly after 60 minutes.

article_faqs.question: Can I use secrets in pull requests from forks?
article_faqs.answer: No. For security, secrets are not available in workflows triggered by pull requests from forks. This prevents malicious PRs from stealing your secrets.

article_faqs.question: Can I temporarily disable protection for an emergency fix?
article_faqs.answer: Admins can bypass rules if 'Do not allow bypassing the above settings' is unchecked. For rulesets, you can define specific bypass actors. However, it is better to create a hotfix branch and fast-track the review process.

article_faqs.question: Can I convert an issue to a discussion?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Open the issue, scroll to the bottom, and click 'Convert to discussion'. The issue will be closed and a new discussion will be created with the same content.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between GitHub Projects and Jira?
article_faqs.answer: GitHub Projects is simpler and tightly integrated with GitHub repos. Jira is more feature-rich but requires a separate tool. For teams already using GitHub, Projects eliminates tool-switching overhead.

article_faqs.question: Is commit signing mandatory?
article_faqs.answer: No, but some organizations require it. GitHub can enforce signed commits through branch protection rules. It is a best practice for security-sensitive projects.

article_faqs.question: Is it safe to store credentials on my computer?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. GCM uses your OS's encrypted credential store. On Windows, it uses the Windows Credential Manager. On macOS, it uses the Keychain. These are encrypted and protected by your system login.

article_faqs.question: What if I lose my phone?
article_faqs.answer: Use one of your saved recovery codes to log in. Then go to Settings to reconfigure 2FA with a new device. If you lost your recovery codes too, contact GitHub Support.

article_faqs.question: Are OAuth apps safe?
article_faqs.answer: Only authorize apps from trusted developers. Review the requested permissions carefully. An app with 'repo' scope can read and modify all your repositories. Regularly audit and revoke unused authorizations.

article_faqs.question: Can I add both SSH keys to the SSH agent?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, add both keys: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_personal && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work. The SSH config file determines which key is used for each host alias.

article_faqs.question: Can I use the same deploy key for multiple repositories?
article_faqs.answer: No. Each deploy key must be unique to a single repository. If you need access to multiple repos, generate a separate key for each one or use a machine user account.

article_faqs.question: Should I use fine-grained or classic tokens?
article_faqs.answer: Fine-grained tokens are recommended for new use cases. They offer better security through repository-scoped access and granular permissions. Classic tokens still work but give broader access than usually needed.

article_faqs.question: Should I use GPG or SSH for signing?
article_faqs.answer: SSH signing is simpler if you already have SSH keys set up. GPG is more established and supports additional features like key expiration and revocation. Both produce the same 'Verified' badge on GitHub.

article_faqs.question: Will I have merge conflicts between remotes?
article_faqs.answer: No. Remotes are independent. Conflicts only happen when you try to merge or pull changes. If different people push to different remotes, you will need to sync manually.

article_faqs.question: Can I convert a regular repo to bare?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Clone the repo as bare: git clone --bare /path/to/regular-repo /path/to/bare-repo.git

article_faqs.question: Will mirroring copy issues and PRs?
article_faqs.answer: No. Git only tracks code, branches, and tags. Issues, PRs, and wiki content are platform-specific. Use GitHub's import tool or APIs to migrate those.

article_faqs.question: Can I push from a shallow clone?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, you can push new commits from a shallow clone. However, some operations like rebasing onto commits not in your shallow history will require unshallowing first.

article_faqs.question: Are submodules difficult to work with?
article_faqs.answer: Submodules add complexity. Team members must remember to init and update submodules. They can cause confusion during merges. Consider alternatives like npm packages, Go modules, or git subtree before using submodules.

article_faqs.question: When should I use subtree instead of submodule?
article_faqs.answer: Use subtree when you want simplicity and don't need frequent upstream updates. Use submodule when the dependency is large, frequently updated, or shared across many projects.

article_faqs.question: What error do I get without upstream?
article_faqs.answer: You'll see 'fatal: The current branch has no upstream branch' when running 'git push' without arguments. Git helpfully suggests the command to set it up.

article_faqs.question: Can I force push to main?
article_faqs.answer: Technically yes, but you should NEVER force push to main or any shared branch. Use branch protection rules to block force pushes on critical branches. Only force push to your own feature branches.

article_faqs.question: Will pruning delete my local branches?
article_faqs.answer: No. Pruning only removes remote-tracking references (origin/branch-name). Your local branches are unaffected. You must delete local branches separately.

article_faqs.question: Does fetching a specific branch save disk space?
article_faqs.answer: It saves bandwidth during the fetch but Git still stores objects efficiently. For significant space savings, combine with --depth (shallow fetch) or --filter (partial clone).

article_faqs.question: Can I recover a file that was never committed?
article_faqs.answer: No. Git can only restore files that were tracked (added and committed) at some point. If a file was never added to Git, it cannot be recovered through Git. Use OS-level recovery tools instead.

article_faqs.question: What if I cannot test a particular commit?
article_faqs.answer: Use 'git bisect skip' to skip the current commit. Git will choose a nearby commit instead. Too many skips can make bisect less efficient.

article_faqs.question: Can I undo a revert?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Revert the revert commit: git revert <revert-commit-hash>. This effectively re-applies the original changes. It sounds strange but it is a legitimate and common technique.

article_faqs.question: Should I revert in forward or reverse order?
article_faqs.answer: When reverting a range, revert in reverse chronological order (newest first). Git does this automatically with the range syntax. Reverting in forward order can cause unnecessary conflicts.

article_faqs.question: Does this affect other files?
article_faqs.answer: No. Restoring a file from a specific commit only changes that one file. All other files remain at their current state.

article_faqs.question: Can I undo git clean?
article_faqs.answer: No. Git clean permanently deletes files that were never tracked. Unlike tracked files, they cannot be recovered from Git history. Always use 'git clean -n' (dry run) first to review what will be deleted.

article_faqs.question: How long does reflog keep entries?
article_faqs.answer: By default, 90 days for reachable entries and 30 days for unreachable ones. You have plenty of time to recover from a bad rebase.

article_faqs.question: What if I made multiple commits on the wrong branch?
article_faqs.answer: Cherry-pick each commit in order: git cherry-pick abc1234 def5678 ghi9012. Then reset the wrong branch back: git reset --hard HEAD~3.

article_faqs.question: What is the difference between unstaging and discarding?
article_faqs.answer: 'git restore --staged file' unstages the file (keeps your edits). 'git restore file' discards your edits entirely (reverts to the last commit). Be careful not to confuse them.

article_faqs.question: Is this safe if I already pushed?
article_faqs.answer: No. Editing older commits rewrites history. If the commits were already pushed, you would need to force push, which affects other collaborators. Only do this for local, unpushed commits.

article_faqs.question: Can two worktrees have the same branch?
article_faqs.answer: No. Each branch can only be checked out in one worktree at a time. This prevents conflicting changes. If you try, Git will give an error.

article_faqs.question: Should I reset instead of reverting a merge?
article_faqs.answer: Only if the merge has not been pushed. 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' removes the merge commit locally. If it was pushed, use revert to avoid rewriting shared history.

article_faqs.question: Is it safe to merge unrelated histories?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, if you understand what you are doing. It simply combines two independent project histories. Make sure you resolve any file conflicts correctly.

article_faqs.question: Why doesn't this happen with all branch switches?
article_faqs.answer: Git only blocks the switch when your uncommitted changes conflict with files that differ between branches. If the changed files are identical on both branches, Git switches cleanly and keeps your changes.

article_faqs.question: I lost commits after leaving detached HEAD. Can I recover them?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Use 'git reflog' to find the lost commit hashes, then create a branch: git branch rescue-branch abc1234

article_faqs.question: Do all team members need LFS installed?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Without LFS installed, team members will see pointer files instead of actual content. Run 'git lfs install' on every machine that will work with the repository.

article_faqs.question: Does cloning with --depth help performance?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. Shallow clones with --depth 1 are much faster to clone and take less disk space. But some operations (blame, log) will have limited history. You can unshallow later if needed.

article_faqs.question: Should I use LF or CRLF in my repository?
article_faqs.answer: Store LF in the repository (Git default). Let each developer's OS handle conversion through autocrlf or .gitattributes. This is the most compatible approach.

article_faqs.question: Can I always recover a corrupted repo?
article_faqs.answer: If you have a remote copy, almost always. Without a remote, it depends on the extent of corruption. Git fsck and reflog can recover many scenarios, but severe disk corruption may result in data loss.

article_faqs.question: Will git gc fix bad objects?
article_faqs.answer: Sometimes. Running 'git gc --prune=now' can clean up unreachable objects. But if a referenced object is truly corrupted, you need to fetch it from a remote or re-clone.

article_faqs.question: Is it safe to delete index.lock?
article_faqs.answer: Yes, as long as no other Git process is actually running. The lock file is temporary and Git will recreate it as needed. Deleting it when no process holds it is completely safe.

article_faqs.question: My hook works locally but fails in CI. Why?
article_faqs.answer: CI environments may not have the same tools installed, or hooks may not be executed at all. Most CI systems run git operations with --no-verify. Configure linting and tests as CI steps instead of relying on hooks in CI.

article_faqs.question: Why do some repos use 'master' and others use 'main'?
article_faqs.answer: Older Git versions defaulted to 'master'. Since 2020, GitHub and Git switched the default to 'main'. Both work the same way — it's just a naming convention. You can set your default with: git config --global init.defaultBranch main

article_faqs.question: My company blocks SSH port 22. Can I still use SSH?
article_faqs.answer: Yes. GitHub allows SSH over port 443: ssh -T -p 443 git@ssh.github.com. Configure it in ~/.ssh/config with 'Host github.com' → 'Hostname ssh.github.com' → 'Port 443'.

article_faqs.question: I get 403 when pushing but cloning works. Why?
article_faqs.answer: Cloning public repos does not require authentication. Pushing always requires authentication. Make sure you are using a valid Personal Access Token (not your password) and that the token has 'repo' scope.

article_faqs.question: Should I avoid submodules?
article_faqs.answer: Submodules add complexity. Consider alternatives: npm/pip packages for libraries, git subtree for simpler embedding, or monorepo approaches. Use submodules only when you truly need to track a specific commit of an external repo.

article_faqs.question: Where can I find good .gitignore templates?
article_faqs.answer: GitHub maintains templates at github.com/github/gitignore for nearly every language and framework. GitHub also offers a .gitignore template selector when creating new repositories.

error_patterns.title: GitHub Authentication Failed
error_patterns.keywords: ["authentication failed","password authentication","support for password authentication was removed"]
error_patterns.solution: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations since August 2021. You need to use either a Personal Access Token (PAT) or SSH key authentication instead. Go to GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens to generate a token.

error_patterns.title: Git Push Rejected
error_patterns.solution: Your local branch is behind the remote branch. The remote has commits that you don't have locally. Pull the latest changes first with 'git pull origin main', resolve any conflicts, then push again.

error_patterns.title: Git Merge Conflict
error_patterns.solution: Open the conflicting files in your text editor and look for conflict markers (<<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>>). Decide which changes to keep, remove the markers, then run 'git add .' and 'git commit'.

error_patterns.title: Detached HEAD State
error_patterns.keywords: ["detached head","head detached","you are in 'detached head' state"]
error_patterns.solution: You are not on any branch. If you want to keep your changes, create a new branch with 'git switch -c new-branch-name'. To go back to an existing branch, use 'git switch main'.

error_patterns.title: Not a Git Repository
error_patterns.keywords: ["fatal: not a git repository","not a git repository"]
error_patterns.solution: You are running a Git command in a directory that has not been initialized as a Git repository. Navigate to the correct project folder, or initialize a new repository with 'git init'.

error_patterns.title: SSH Permission Denied
error_patterns.solution: Your SSH key is not set up correctly or not added to your GitHub account. Generate a new SSH key with 'ssh-keygen -t ed25519' and add the public key to GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys.

error_patterns.title: Remote Origin Already Exists
error_patterns.solution: You are trying to add a remote named 'origin' but one already exists. Use 'git remote set-url origin <new-url>' to update it, or 'git remote remove origin' to remove it first.

error_patterns.title: Pathspec Error – File or Branch Not Found
error_patterns.solution: The file or branch name you specified doesn't exist. Check for typos in the name. Use 'git branch -a' to see all branches or 'ls' to list files in the current directory.

error_patterns.title: Branch Ahead of Remote
error_patterns.keywords: ["your branch is ahead","ahead of","use git push"]
error_patterns.solution: Your local branch has commits that haven't been pushed to the remote. Run 'git push origin <branch-name>' to upload your commits to the remote repository.

error_patterns.title: Branch Behind Remote
error_patterns.solution: The remote branch has commits that you don't have locally. Run 'git pull origin <branch-name>' to download and merge the latest changes.
